chapters.title: Letter of Dedication
paragraphs:
TO THE MOST WISE AND ILLUSTRIOUS THE DEAN AND DOCTORS OF THE SACRED FACULTY OF THEOLOGY OF PARIS.

GENTLEMEN,

1. The reason that moves me to present this Treatise to you is so sound, and once you understand its design I am confident you will agree there is such valid ground for taking it under your protection, that I can find no better way to commend it to you than to state briefly the end I set for myself in writing it.

2. I have always held that the two questions concerning God and the Soul are foremost among those that ought to be settled by Philosophy rather than by Theology. For although it is enough for us, the faithful, to hold as matters of faith that the human soul does not perish with the body, and that God exists, it nevertheless seems impossible ever to persuade unbelievers of the reality of any religion, or of almost any moral virtue, unless those two truths are first proved to them by natural reason. And since in this life vice is often offered greater rewards than virtue, few would prefer the right to the useful, were they restrained neither by the fear of God nor the expectation of another life. It is quite true that we should believe in the existence of God because it is taught in the sacred Scriptures, and that the sacred Scriptures should be believed because they come from God — for since faith is a gift of God, the same Being who bestows the grace that lets us believe other things can also bestow the grace that lets us believe in his own existence. Yet this argument cannot be put to unbelievers, who would treat the reasoning as circular. I have observed that you, along with all other theologians, not only affirm that natural reason is sufficient to prove the existence of God, but also infer from sacred Scripture that the knowledge of God is much clearer than the knowledge of many created things, and that it is in fact so easy to acquire that those who lack it are blameworthy. This is plain from the words of the Book of Wisdom, chapter xiii: 'Howbeit they are not to be excused; for if their understanding was so great that they could discern the world and the creatures, why did they not rather find out the Lord thereof?' And in Romans, chapter i, it is said that they are without excuse; and again, in the same place, by the words 'That which may be known of God is manifest in them' — we seem to be told that all that can be known of God may be made manifest by reasons drawn from no other source than the inspection of our own minds. I have therefore thought it not unfitting to inquire how, and by what way, without going outside ourselves, God may be known more easily and more certainly than the things of the world.

3. As for the Soul, although many have judged that its nature could not be easily discovered, and some have even ventured to say that human reason leads to the conclusion that it perishes with the body, and that the contrary opinion can be held through faith alone, nevertheless, since the Lateran Council under Leo X (in session viii) condemned these views and expressly enjoined Christian philosophers to refute their arguments and establish the truth as best they can, I have ventured to attempt it in this work.

4. Moreover, I am aware that most of the irreligious deny the existence of God, and the distinctness of the human soul from the body, for no other reason than because these points, as they allege, have never yet been demonstrated. Now, although I am by no means of their opinion, but on the contrary hold that almost all the proofs adduced on these questions by great men possess, when rightly understood, the force of demonstrations, and that it is next to impossible to discover new ones, yet there is, I believe, no more useful service to be performed in Philosophy than for someone, once and for all, to seek out carefully the best of these reasons and set them out so accurately and clearly that, from then on, it might be plain to all that they are real demonstrations. And finally, since many people who knew that I had cultivated a certain Method for resolving all kinds of difficulties in the sciences — a Method not new (there being nothing older than truth), but one I had used successfully in other matters — were greatly desirous of this, I judged it to be my duty to put it to the test on the present subject as well.

5. The sum of what I have been able to accomplish on the subject is contained in this Treatise. I did not here attempt to gather every reason that might be offered as proof — that is unnecessary except in matters where no single proof of adequate certainty is available. Instead I treated only the first and chief proofs, and treated them in such a way that I now venture to propose them as demonstrations of the highest certainty and evidence. I will add that they are such as to convince me there is no way open to the human mind by which superior proofs could ever be discovered. The importance of the subject, and the glory of God to which all this relates, oblige me to speak here a little more freely about myself than I am accustomed to do. Yet whatever certitude and evidence I may find in these demonstrations, I cannot persuade myself that they lie within the grasp of all readers. Just as in geometry there are many demonstrations by Archimedes, Apollonius, Pappus, and others, which, though received by all as evident and certain (because they manifestly contain nothing that, considered by itself, is not very easy to understand, and no consequents that fail to follow strictly from their antecedents), are nevertheless understood by very few, because they are somewhat long and demand the reader's full attention — so too here. Although I consider the demonstrations I employ to be equal or even superior to the geometrical in certitude and evidence, I am afraid that they will not be adequately understood by many, both because they too are somewhat long and involved, and chiefly because they require the mind to be entirely free from prejudice, and able to detach itself easily from the commerce of the senses. To speak the truth, the aptitude for metaphysical study is less common than for geometry. There is also this further difference: in geometry everyone is persuaded that nothing is normally advanced of which there is not a certain demonstration, so those only partly versed in it err more often in agreeing with what is false (out of a desire to seem to understand it) than in denying what is true. In philosophy, on the other hand, where it is believed that all is doubtful, few sincerely give themselves to the search for truth; far more seek the reputation of bold thinkers by audaciously attacking truths of the greatest importance.

6. For this reason, whatever force my reasonings may possess, I do not expect them, just because they belong to philosophy, to have much effect on the minds of men, unless you extend to them your patronage and approval. But your Faculty is held in such great esteem by all, and the name of SORBONNE carries such authority, that not only in matters of faith but even in matters of human philosophy the judgment of no other society — after the Sacred Councils — has received such deference. The universal conviction is that nowhere else is greater perspicacity and solidity to be found, nor greater wisdom and integrity in passing judgment. I do not doubt, then, that if you will but condescend to give this Treatise enough regard, first, to correct it (for mindful not only of my humanity but chiefly of my ignorance, I do not claim it is free from errors); next, to supply what is lacking in it, perfect what is incomplete, and give fuller illustration where it is needed, or at least to point out these defects to me so that I may try to remedy them; and finally, when the reasonings contained in it — by which the existence of God and the distinction of the human soul from the body are established — have been brought to such a degree of clarity that they may be regarded as exact demonstrations (which I am assured they admit), if you will deign to grant them the authority of your approbation, and give public testimony of their truth and certainty — I do not doubt, I say, that all the errors ever entertained on these questions will very soon be wiped from men's minds. For truth itself will readily lead the rest of the ingenious and the learned to subscribe to your judgment; and your authority will cause the atheists, who are generally sciolists rather than ingenious or learned, to lay aside the spirit of contradiction, and lead them perhaps to do battle in their own persons for reasonings which they find considered demonstrations by all men of genius, lest they seem not to understand them; and finally, the rest of mankind will readily trust to so many testimonies, and there will no longer be anyone who would venture to doubt either the existence of God or the real distinction of mind and body. It is for you, in your singular wisdom, to judge the importance of establishing such beliefs, [who are aware of the disorders that doubt of these truths produces]. But it would not become me here to commend at greater length the cause of God and of religion to you, who have always proved the strongest support of the Catholic Church.

chapters.title: Preface to the Reader
paragraphs: 1. I already touched briefly on the questions concerning the existence of God and the nature of the human soul in the 'Discourse on the Method of rightly conducting the Reason, and seeking Truth in the Sciences,' published in French in 1637 — not, however, with the intention of treating them fully there, but only in passing, so that I might learn from my readers' judgment how I should afterward handle them. These questions seemed to me of such importance that they deserved more than a single examination, and the path I follow in discussing them is so little trodden, and so remote from the ordinary route, that I thought it inadvisable to set it out at greater length in French, in a discourse that might be read by anyone, lest even feeble minds should believe they too could enter upon it.

2. But since, in the 'Discourse on Method,' I had asked all who found anything in my writings deserving criticism to do me the favor of pointing it out, I can report that no objections worth noting were raised against what I said there on these questions, except two, to which I will here reply briefly before undertaking their more detailed discussion.

3. The first objection is this: although the human mind, when it reflects on itself, does not perceive itself to be anything other than a thinking thing, it does not follow that its nature or essence consists only in being a thing that thinks — so that the word ONLY would exclude every other thing that might also be said to belong to the nature of the mind. To this I reply that I did not, in that passage, intend to exclude these things according to the order of truth in the matter itself (which I was not then discussing), but only according to the order of thought (perception). My meaning was that I clearly apprehended nothing, so far as I was conscious, as belonging to my essence, except that I was a thinking thing — that is, a thing possessing within itself the faculty of thinking. But I will show later how, from the consciousness that nothing besides thinking belongs to the essence of the mind, it follows that in truth nothing else belongs to it.

4. The second objection is that it does not follow, from my possessing the idea of a thing more perfect than I am, that the idea itself is more perfect than I, much less that what is represented by the idea actually exists. I reply that there is here an ambiguity in the term idea. It may be taken either materially, for an act of the understanding, in which sense it cannot be said to be more perfect than I; or objectively, for the thing represented by that act, which, even if it is not supposed to exist outside my understanding, may nevertheless be more perfect than myself by reason of its essence. But later in this treatise I will show more fully how, from my possessing the idea of a thing more perfect than myself, it follows that this thing really exists.

5. Besides these two objections, I have indeed seen two treatises of considerable length on this matter. In them, however, my conclusions far more than my premises were attacked, and by arguments borrowed from the commonplaces of the atheists. Since arguments of that sort can make no impression on minds that rightly understand my reasonings, and since the judgments of many are so irrational and weak that they are persuaded rather by the opinions first presented to them — however false and contrary to reason — than by a true and solid refutation received afterward, I am unwilling to reply to these strictures here, for fear of first having to state them. I will only say, in general, that all the atheists commonly allege in favor of the non-existence of God arises continually from one of two things: either ascribing human affections to the Deity, or attributing to our minds such vigor and wisdom that we presume to determine and comprehend both what God can and what God ought to do. Everything they allege will give us no difficulty, provided only we keep in mind that our minds must be considered finite, while the Deity is incomprehensible and infinite.

6. Now that I have, in some measure, tested men's opinions of my work, I again undertake to treat of God and the human soul, and at the same time to discuss the principles of the entire First Philosophy — without, however, expecting any commendation from the crowd, or a wide circle of readers. On the contrary, I would advise no one to read this work except those who are able and willing to meditate with me in earnest, to detach their minds from commerce with the senses, and likewise to free themselves from all prejudice. Such individuals are, as I well know, remarkably rare. As for those who, without caring to grasp the order and connection of the reasonings, will study only detached clauses for the sake of petty but noisy criticism — as many do — I may say that such readers will not profit much from this treatise. And although they may perhaps find occasion for cavilling in several places, they will hardly raise any pressing objections, or any deserving of reply.

7. But since I do not promise to satisfy others on all these subjects at first sight, nor presume so far as to believe I could foresee every difficulty each reader might find, I will first set out, in the Meditations, those considerations by which I feel convinced I have arrived at certain and evident knowledge of the truth — in order to test whether the reasonings that have prevailed with me will also prove effective in convincing others. I will then reply to the objections of certain men illustrious for their genius and learning, to whom these Meditations were sent for criticism before being committed to the press; for these objections are so numerous and varied that I venture to anticipate that nothing — at least nothing of any importance — will readily occur to any mind that has not been touched on in them. Hence I earnestly entreat my readers not to form any judgment on the questions raised in the Meditations until they have taken care to read the whole of the Objections, with the relevant Replies.

chapters.title: Synopsis of the Six Following Meditations
paragraphs: 1. In the First Meditation I set out the grounds on which we may doubt all things in general, and material objects in particular, at least so long as we have no firmer foundations for the sciences than those we have so far possessed. The usefulness of so general a doubt may not be obvious at first sight, but it is in fact of the greatest value: it frees us from all prejudice, offers the easiest path by which the mind may withdraw itself from the senses, and finally makes it impossible for us to doubt anything we afterward discover to be true.

2. In the Second, the mind, exercising the freedom proper to it, supposes the non-existence of every object about which it has even the slightest doubt — and finds that, all the while, it must itself exist. This point is likewise of the highest importance, for it allows the mind to distinguish easily what belongs to itself, that is, to its intellectual nature, from what is to be referred to the body. But since some readers may, at this stage, expect a statement of the reasons that establish the immortality of the soul, I think it proper to make them aware that I aimed to write nothing for which I could not give exact demonstration, and therefore felt obliged to adopt an order similar to the one used by geometers — namely, to lay out everything on which the proposition in question depends before drawing any conclusion about it. The first and chief prerequisite for the knowledge of the immortality of the soul is our being able to form the clearest possible conception (conceptus — concept) of the soul itself, one absolutely distinct from all our notions of body; and how this is to be accomplished is shown there. We also need the assurance that everything we clearly and distinctly think is true (really exists) in that very mode in which we think it — and this could not be established before the Fourth Meditation. Further, for the same purpose, we must possess a distinct conception of corporeal nature, which is given partly in the Second and partly in the Fifth and Sixth Meditations. Finally, from these grounds we are forced to conclude that all those objects which are clearly and distinctly conceived to be diverse substances — such as mind and body — are substances really and mutually distinct; this inference is made in the Sixth Meditation. The absolute distinction of mind and body is also confirmed in this Second Meditation by showing that we cannot conceive of body except as divisible, while on the other hand we cannot conceive of mind except as indivisible. We cannot conceive of half a mind, as we can of any body however small, so that the natures of these two substances must be regarded not merely as diverse but in some measure as contraries. I have not, however, pursued this discussion further in the present treatise, both because these considerations are enough to show that the destruction of the mind does not follow from the corruption of the body — and thus to give men hope of a future life — and also because the premises from which we may rightly infer the immortality of the soul require an explanation of the whole of Physics: first, to establish that, generally, all substances — that is, all things that can exist only as a result of having been created by God — are in their own nature incorruptible, and can never cease to be, unless God himself, by refusing his concurrence, reduces them to nothing; and second, that body, taken generally, is a substance, and therefore can never perish, but that the human body, insofar as it differs from other bodies, is constituted only by a certain configuration of its members and by other accidents of that kind, whereas the human mind is not made up of accidents but is a pure substance. For although all the accidents of the mind change — although, for example, it thinks certain things, wills others, and perceives still others — the mind itself does not vary with these changes; the human body, by contrast, is no longer the same if a change occurs in the form of any of its parts. From which it follows that the body may indeed perish without difficulty, but that the mind is by its own nature immortal.

3. In the Third Meditation I have, I think, unfolded at sufficient length my chief argument for the existence of God. But since I was there anxious to avoid comparisons drawn from material objects — so as to withdraw the reader's mind from the senses as much as possible — numerous obscurities perhaps remain, which I trust will be entirely removed afterward in the Replies to the Objections. Among other things, it may be difficult to understand how the idea of an absolutely perfect being, which is found in our minds, possesses so much objective reality [i.e. participates by representation in so many degrees of being and perfection] that it must be held to arise from an absolutely perfect cause. This is illustrated in the Replies by the comparison of a highly perfect machine, the idea of which exists in the mind of some workman: just as the objective (i.e. representative) perfection of this idea must have some cause — namely, the science of the workman, or of some other person from whom he received the idea — in the same way the idea of God, which is found in us, demands God himself as its cause.

4. In the Fourth Meditation it is shown that everything we clearly and distinctly perceive (apprehend) is true, and at the same time it is explained in what the nature of error consists — points that need to be known both to confirm the preceding truths and to better understand those that follow. It must be observed, however, that I do not there treat of Sin at all, that is, of error committed in the pursuit of good and evil, but only of the kind that arises in determining the true and the false. Nor do I refer to matters of faith, or to the conduct of life, but only to what concerns speculative truths — those known by the natural light alone.

5. In the Fifth Meditation, besides an account of corporeal nature taken generically, a new demonstration is given of the existence of God — not free, perhaps, any more than the former, from certain difficulties, but the solution to these will be found in the Replies to the Objections. I further show in what sense it is true that the certitude of geometrical demonstrations themselves depends on the knowledge of God.

6. Finally, in the Sixth Meditation, the act of the understanding (intellectio) is distinguished from that of the imagination (imaginatio); the marks of this distinction are described; the human mind is shown to be really distinct from the body and yet to be so closely conjoined with it as to form, with it, what amounts to a unity. The whole range of errors that arise from the senses is reviewed, and the means of avoiding them are pointed out. Finally, all the grounds are set forth from which the existence of material objects may be inferred — not because I thought them of great use in establishing what they prove (namely, that there really is a world, that men have bodies, and the like — truths no one of sound mind ever seriously doubted), but because, from a close consideration of them, it is seen that they are neither as strong nor as clear as the reasonings that lead us to the knowledge of our mind and of God. The latter are, of all things that come under human knowledge, the most certain and manifest — a conclusion that was my single aim in these Meditations to establish. For this reason I here omit mention of the various other questions I also had occasion to consider in the course of the discussion.

chapters.title: Meditation I — Of the Things of Which We May Doubt
paragraphs: 1. Several years have now passed since I first noticed that, even from my youth, I had accepted many false opinions as true, and that everything I afterward built on such principles was therefore highly doubtful. From that time on I was convinced that I had to undertake, once in my life, to rid myself of all the opinions I had adopted, and to begin anew the work of building from the foundation, if I wanted to establish anything firm and lasting in the sciences. But the project seemed so large that I waited until I had reached an age mature enough to leave me no hope that any later stage of life would find me better fitted to carry out my design. For this reason I have delayed so long that I would now think myself in the wrong if I went on consuming in deliberation any of the time that remains for action. Today, then, since I have happily freed my mind from all cares [and am happily disturbed by no passions], and since I am in the secure possession of leisure in a peaceable retirement, I will at last apply myself, earnestly and freely, to the general overthrow of all my former opinions.

2. To this end, it will not be necessary for me to show that they are all false — a point I shall perhaps never reach. Even now my reason convinces me that I ought to withhold belief no less carefully from what is not entirely certain and indubitable than from what is plainly false. So it will be enough to justify rejecting them all if I find in each some ground for doubt. Nor will it be necessary, for this purpose, to deal with each belief individually — that would be a truly endless labor. But since the removal of the foundation necessarily brings down the whole edifice with it, I will at once attack the principles on which all my former beliefs rested.

3. Everything I have so far accepted as possessing the highest truth and certainty, I received either from the senses or through them. I have observed, however, that the senses sometimes mislead us; and it is the part of prudence not to place absolute confidence in anything by which we have once been deceived.

4. But it may be objected that, although the senses occasionally mislead us about minute objects, or about things so far removed that they are beyond close observation, there are still many other reports of theirs whose truth it is plainly impossible to doubt — for example, that I am here, seated by the fire, dressed in a winter dressing gown, holding this piece of paper in my hands, and so on. How could I deny that these hands and this body are mine, without classing myself with madmen whose brains are so disordered and clouded by dark bilious vapors that they obstinately insist they are kings when they are utterly poor, or clothed [in gold] and purple when they are naked, or that their head is made of clay, their body of glass, or that they are gourds? I would surely be no less mad than they if I regulated my conduct by such extravagant examples.

5. Yet I must here consider that I am a man, and that, accordingly, I am in the habit of sleeping, and of representing to myself in dreams the very same things — and sometimes things still less probable — that the insane think they perceive while awake. How often have I dreamt that I was here, dressed and seated by the fire, when in fact I was lying undressed in bed? At this very moment, however, I am surely looking at this paper with eyes wide open; the head I am moving is not asleep; I extend this hand consciously and on purpose, and I feel it; what happens in sleep is never as distinct as all this. But I cannot forget that on other occasions I have been deceived in sleep by similar illusions; and as I consider those cases attentively, I see so clearly that there are no certain marks by which the waking state can ever be distinguished from sleep, that I am greatly astonished — and in my amazement I almost convince myself that I am dreaming now.

6. Let us suppose, then, that we are dreaming, and that all these particulars — the opening of the eyes, the movement of the head, the stretching out of the hands — are merely illusions, and even that we really possess neither a whole body nor hands such as we see. It must still at least be admitted that the things which appear to us in sleep are like painted images that could not have been formed except in the likeness of realities. Therefore, those general objects — eyes, a head, hands, an entire body — are not simply imaginary but really existent. For even when painters strive to represent sirens and satyrs in the most fantastic and extraordinary forms, they cannot bestow upon them natures absolutely new; they can only make a kind of medley of the limbs of different animals. Or if they happen to imagine something so novel that nothing similar has ever been seen before — something purely fictitious and absolutely false — it is at least certain that the colors of which it is composed are real. By the same principle, although these general objects — [a body], eyes, a head, hands, and the like — may be imaginary, we are nevertheless absolutely forced to admit the reality of certain other things still simpler and more universal, out of which (just as out of certain real colors) all the images of things, whether true and real or false and fantastic, that are found in our consciousness (cogitatio) are formed.

7. To this class of objects seem to belong corporeal nature in general and its extension; the shape of extended things, their quantity or size, and their number; as also the place in which, and the time during which, they exist, and other things of the same sort.

8. We will perhaps not reason illegitimately, then, if we conclude from this that Physics, Astronomy, Medicine, and all the other sciences whose object is composite things are indeed of a doubtful character, but that Arithmetic, Geometry, and the other sciences of that same class — which deal only with the simplest and most general objects, and barely inquire whether or not these really exist — contain something that is certain and indubitable. For whether I am awake or dreaming, it remains true that two and three make five, and that a square has only four sides; nor does it seem possible that truths so apparent could ever fall under a suspicion of falsity [or uncertainty].

9. Nevertheless, the belief that there is a God who is all-powerful, and who created me as I am, has long held steady possession of my mind. How then do I know that he has not arranged things so that there is no earth, no sky, no extended thing, no shape, no size, no place, while at the same time providing for [the rise in me of the perceptions of all these things, and] the conviction that they exist exactly as I perceive them? Furthermore, since I sometimes judge that others go wrong about matters they think they know perfectly, how do I know I am not myself deceived every time I add two and three, or count the sides of a square, or form some still simpler judgment — if anything simpler can be imagined? But perhaps the Deity has not been willing that I should be thus deceived, for he is said to be supremely good. Yet if it were inconsistent with God's goodness to have created me subject to constant deception, it would seem equally inconsistent with his goodness to allow me to be deceived even occasionally — and yet plainly this is permitted.

10. Some might perhaps be inclined to deny the existence of so powerful a Being rather than believe that there is nothing certain. But for the moment let us refrain from opposing this opinion, and grant that everything said here of a Deity is a fable. Nevertheless, in whatever way I am supposed to have come into the state in which I exist — by fate, or by chance, or by an endless series of antecedents and consequents, or by any other means — it is clear that, since to be deceived and to err is a certain defect, the probability of my being imperfect enough to be the constant victim of deception will increase exactly in proportion as the power of whatever cause is assigned my origin is diminished. To these arguments I have nothing at all to reply, and I am at last forced to admit that there is nothing of all I formerly believed to be true of which it is impossible to doubt — and this not from thoughtlessness or levity, but from cogent and well-considered reasons. So from now on, if I want to discover anything certain, I ought to refrain from assenting to those same opinions no less carefully than to what might be shown to be plainly false.

11. But it is not enough to have made these observations; care must also be taken to keep them in mind. For those old and habitual opinions keep returning — long and familiar use giving them the right to occupy my mind, almost against my will, and to subdue my belief. I shall not lose the habit of deferring to them and trusting them so long as I regard them as what in truth they are: opinions somewhat doubtful, as I have already shown, but still highly probable, and far more reasonable to believe than to deny. For this reason I am convinced that I shall not be doing wrong if, deliberately taking the opposite view, I become my own deceiver — supposing, for a time, that all those opinions are entirely false and imaginary — until at last, having balanced my old prejudices against my new ones, my judgment will no longer be turned aside by twisted habit from the path that may lead to the perception of truth. For I am sure that meanwhile no peril or error will arise from this course, and that I cannot for the present yield too much to distrust, since what I now seek is not action but knowledge.

12. I will suppose, then, not that the Deity, who is sovereignly good and the source of truth, but that some malignant demon, at once supremely powerful and deceitful, has used all his cunning to deceive me. I will suppose that the sky, the air, the earth, colors, shapes, sounds, and all external things are nothing more than the illusions of dreams, by which this being has laid snares for my credulity. I will regard myself as having no hands, no eyes, no flesh, no blood, no senses at all, and as merely believing falsely that I have these things. I will hold resolutely to this stance, and even if it is not in my power, by these means, to arrive at the knowledge of truth, I shall at least do what is in my power: [suspend my judgment], and guard with settled purpose against giving my assent to anything false, against being imposed upon by this deceiver, whatever his power and cunning. But the undertaking is arduous, and a certain indolence insensibly leads me back to my ordinary way of life. Just as the captive who in his dreams was enjoying an imaginary liberty, when he begins to suspect that it is only a vision, dreads waking and conspires with the agreeable illusions to prolong the deception, so I of my own accord fall back into the round of my former beliefs, and I fear to rouse myself from my slumber, lest the time of laborious wakefulness that would follow this quiet rest, instead of bringing any light of day, should prove unable to dispel the darkness that will arise from the difficulties just raised.

chapters.title: Meditation II — Of the Nature of the Human Mind, And That It Is More Easily Known Than the Body
paragraphs: 1. Yesterday's Meditation has filled my mind with so many doubts that it is no longer in my power to forget them. Nor can I see, meanwhile, any principle by which they might be resolved; and just as if I had fallen all of a sudden into very deep water, I am so disconcerted that I can neither plant my feet firmly on the bottom nor support myself by swimming on the surface. I will nevertheless make an effort, and try once more the path I entered yesterday — that is, set aside everything that admits of the slightest doubt, no less than if I had found it absolutely false; and I will keep on this track until I find something certain, or at least, if I can do nothing more, until I know with certainty that there is nothing certain. Archimedes, in order to move the entire globe from its place, asked only for one firm and immovable point. So too I shall be entitled to the highest expectations if I am fortunate enough to discover even one thing that is certain and indubitable.

2. I suppose, then, that all the things I see are false (fictitious); I believe that none of those objects which my fallacious memory represents ever existed; I suppose that I have no senses; I believe that body, shape, extension, motion, and place are merely fictions of my mind. What then is there that can be considered true? Perhaps only this: that there is absolutely nothing certain.

3. But how do I know that there is not something altogether different from the objects I have just listed, of which the slightest doubt is impossible? Is there not a God — or some being, by whatever name I designate him — who causes these thoughts to arise in my mind? But why suppose such a being, when perhaps I am myself capable of producing them? Am I, then, not at least something? But I have already denied that I have senses or a body. Still, I hesitate — for what follows from that? Am I so dependent on the body and the senses that without them I cannot exist? But I had convinced myself that there was nothing in the world — no sky, no earth, no minds, no bodies; was I not therefore also convinced that I did not exist? Far from it: I certainly did exist, since I was the one being convinced. But there is some being — I know not who — at once supremely powerful and supremely cunning, who is constantly using all his ingenuity to deceive me. Without doubt, then, I exist, since I am being deceived; and let him deceive me as he may, he can never bring it about that I am nothing, so long as I am conscious that I am something. So that, when all things have been weighed and carefully considered, this proposition (pronunciatum) — I am, I exist — is necessarily true each time it is spoken by me, or conceived in my mind.

4. But I do not yet know with sufficient clarity what I am, even though I am sure that I am. So now I must take care not to thoughtlessly substitute some other object for what is properly myself, and so wander from the truth even in that knowledge (cognition) which I hold to be the most certain and evident of all. For this reason I will now consider afresh what I formerly believed myself to be, before I entered on this present train of thought; and from my previous opinion I will cut away everything that can in the least be undermined by the grounds of doubt I have advanced, so that at last there remains only what is certain and indubitable.

5. What, then, did I formerly think I was? Undoubtedly I judged that I was a man. But what is a man? Shall I say a rational animal? Surely not — for then I would have to inquire at once into what is meant by animal and what by rational, and so, from a single question, I would slip imperceptibly into others, more difficult than the first; and I have no leisure now to waste my time on subtleties of that kind. I prefer to attend here to the thoughts that arose spontaneously in my mind, inspired by my own nature alone, when I applied myself to consider what I was. In the first place, then, I thought that I had a face, hands, arms, and the whole frame of limbs that appears in a corpse — what I called by the name of body. It also occurred to me that I was nourished, that I walked, that I perceived, that I thought; and all these actions I referred to the soul. But what the soul itself was, I either did not stop to consider, or, if I did, I imagined it to be something extremely rare and subtle — like wind, or flame, or ether — spread through my grosser parts. As for the body, I did not even doubt its nature, but thought I knew it distinctly; and if I had wanted to describe it according to the notions I then held, I would have explained myself this way: by body I understand whatever can be bounded by a certain shape; whatever can be enclosed in a certain place, and so fill a certain space as to exclude every other body from it; whatever can be perceived by touch, sight, hearing, taste, or smell; whatever can be moved in various ways — not, indeed, by itself, but by something foreign that touches it [and from which it receives the impression]. For the power of self-motion, like that of perceiving and thinking, I held to be in no way pertaining to the nature of body; on the contrary, I was somewhat astonished to find such faculties existing in some bodies.

6. But [as for myself, what can I now say that I am], since I suppose there exists an extremely powerful and — if I may so speak — malignant being, whose whole effort is directed toward deceiving me? Can I affirm that I possess any one of all those attributes I have just spoken of as belonging to the nature of body? After attentively considering them in my own mind, I find none of them that can properly be said to belong to me. To recount them would be idle and tedious. Let us pass, then, to the attributes of the soul. The first mentioned were the powers of nutrition and of walking; but if it is true that I have no body, it is equally true that I am capable neither of walking nor of being nourished. Perception is another attribute of the soul; but perception too is impossible without a body; and besides, in sleep I have often believed I perceived objects that I afterward observed I did not really perceive. Thinking is another attribute of the soul; and here I find what truly belongs to me. This alone is inseparable from me. I am — I exist: this is certain; but for how long? As long as I think; for it might perhaps happen that, if I wholly ceased to think, I should at the same time wholly cease to be. I now admit nothing that is not necessarily true. I am, therefore, precisely speaking, only a thinking thing — that is, a mind (mens sive animus), an understanding, or a reason, terms whose meaning was previously unknown to me. I am, however, a real thing, and really existent; but what thing? The answer was: a thinking thing.

7. The question now arises: am I anything besides? I will stir up my imagination to see whether I am not still something more than a thinking being. Now it is plain that I am not the assemblage of limbs called the human body; I am not a thin and penetrating air diffused through these limbs, nor wind, nor flame, nor vapor, nor breath, nor any of the things I can imagine — for I supposed that all these did not exist, and, without changing the supposition, I find that I still feel sure of my existence. But it is true, perhaps, that those very things I suppose not to exist, because they are unknown to me, are not in truth different from myself, whom I do know. This is a point I cannot determine, and I will not now enter into any dispute about it. I can only judge of things known to me: I am conscious that I exist, and I, who know that I exist, am inquiring into what I am. It is, however, perfectly certain that the knowledge of my existence, taken thus precisely, does not depend on things whose existence is as yet unknown to me — and consequently it does not depend on any of the things I can feign in imagination. Moreover, the very phrase, I form an image (effingo), reminds me of my error; for I would indeed be forming one if I were to imagine myself to be anything, since to imagine is nothing more than to contemplate the shape or image of a corporeal thing. But I already know that I exist, and that it is possible at the same time that all those images, and indeed everything that pertains to the nature of body, are merely dreams [or chimeras]. From this I see that it is no more reasonable to say, 'I will excite my imagination so that I may know more distinctly what I am,' than it would be to say, 'I am now awake, and perceive something real; but because my perception is not sufficiently clear, I will deliberately go to sleep so that my dreams may represent to me the object of my perception with more truth and clarity.' I therefore know that nothing of all that I can grasp by imagination belongs to the knowledge I have of myself, and that I must with the utmost care recall the mind from this mode of thinking, so that it may know its own nature with perfect distinctness.

8. But what then am I? A thinking thing, it has been said. But what is a thinking thing? It is a thing that doubts, understands, [conceives], affirms, denies, wills, refuses; that also imagines, and perceives.

9. Surely it is not little, if all these properties belong to my nature. But why should they not belong to it? Am I not the very being who now doubts almost everything; who nevertheless understands and conceives certain things; who affirms one of them alone as true and denies the rest; who desires to know more of them, and does not wish to be deceived; who imagines many things, sometimes even against his will; and who likewise perceives many things, as if through the senses? Is any of this less true than that I am, even if I were always dreaming, and even if the one who gave me being employed all his ingenuity to deceive me? Is there any one of these attributes that can properly be distinguished from my thought, or said to be separate from myself? It is so self-evident that it is I who doubt, I who understand, and I who desire, that there is no need to add anything to make it clearer. And I am no less certainly the same being who imagines; for although it may be (as I supposed before) that nothing I imagine is true, still the power of imagination does not cease really to exist in me and to form part of my thought. Finally, I am the same being who perceives — that is, who apprehends certain objects as if by the organs of sense — for I really do see light, hear noise, feel heat. But it will be said that these presentations are false, and that I am dreaming. Let it be so. At all events, it is certain that I seem to see light, hear noise, and feel heat; this cannot be false; and this is what in me is properly called perceiving (sentire), which is nothing other than thinking.

10. From this I begin to know what I am with somewhat greater clarity and distinctness than before. But it still seems to me — and I cannot help believing — that corporeal things, whose images are formed by thought [and which fall under the senses], and are examined by the same, are known with much greater distinctness than that I-know-not-what part of myself which cannot be imagined. Although it may seem strange to say that I know and understand more distinctly things whose existence appears doubtful to me, that are unknown to me, and do not belong to me, than others of whose reality I am convinced, that are known to me, and that belong to my own nature — in a word, more distinctly than I know myself. But I see clearly what the case is. My mind is apt to wander, and will not yet be confined within the limits of truth. So let us once more leave the mind to itself, and grant it every kind of freedom [allow it to consider the objects that appear to it from outside], so that, after we have afterward gently and at the right moment drawn it back from these [and fixed it on the consideration of its own being and of the properties it finds in itself], it may be more easily controlled.

11. Let us therefore now consider the objects that are commonly thought to be [most easily and] most distinctly known — namely, the bodies we touch and see; not, indeed, bodies in general, for these general notions are usually somewhat more confused, but one body in particular. Take, for example, this piece of wax. It is quite fresh, having been only recently taken from the beehive; it has not yet lost the sweetness of the honey it contained; it still retains some of the scent of the flowers from which it was gathered; its color, shape, and size are apparent (to the sight); it is hard, cold, easily handled; and it sounds when struck with the finger. In short, all that is needed to make a body as distinctly known as possible is found in the one before me. But while I am speaking, let it be placed near the fire — what remained of the taste exhales, the smell evaporates, the color changes, its shape is destroyed, its size grows greater, it becomes liquid, it grows hot, it can hardly be handled, and when struck it gives off no sound. Does the same wax still remain after this change? It must be admitted that it does; no one doubts it, no one judges otherwise. What then was it that I knew so distinctly in the piece of wax? Surely it could not have been any of those things I observed by the senses, since everything that fell under taste, smell, sight, touch, and hearing has changed, and yet the same wax remains.

12. It was perhaps what I now think — namely, that this wax was neither the sweetness of honey, nor the pleasant scent of flowers, nor the whiteness, nor the shape, nor the sound, but only a body that a little before showed itself to me under these forms, and that is now perceived under others. But, to speak precisely, what is it that I imagine when I think of it this way? Let it be considered carefully, and, cutting away everything that does not belong to the wax, let us see what remains. There certainly remains nothing except something extended, flexible, and movable. But what is meant by flexible and movable? Is it that I imagine that the piece of wax, being round, is capable of becoming square, or of passing from a square into a triangular shape? Surely not, because I conceive that it admits of an infinity of similar changes; and I am unable to compass this infinity by imagination. So this conception I have of the wax is not the product of the faculty of imagination. But what now is this extension? Is it not also unknown? It becomes greater when the wax is melted, greater when it is boiled, and greater still as the heat increases; and I should not conceive [clearly and] truly the wax as it is, if I did not suppose that the piece we are considering admits of an even wider variety of extension than I have ever imagined. I must therefore admit that I cannot even grasp by imagination what the piece of wax is, and that the mind alone (mens, Lat., entendement, F.) perceives it. I am speaking of this piece in particular; for as to wax in general, the point is even more evident. But what is the piece of wax that can be perceived only by the [understanding, or] mind? It is certainly the same that I see, touch, imagine; and, in short, the same I believed it to be from the beginning. But — and this is important to observe — the perception of it is not an act of sight, of touch, or of imagination, and never was either of these, though it may have seemed so before. It is simply an intuition (inspectio) of the mind, which may be imperfect and confused, as it formerly was, or very clear and distinct, as it is now, depending on whether the attention is directed more or less to the elements that the wax contains and of which it is composed.

13. Yet I am greatly astonished when I observe [the weakness of my mind, and] its proneness to error. For although, without giving expression at all to what I think, I consider all this in my own mind, words still occasionally hinder me, and I am almost led into error by the terms of ordinary language. We say, for example, that we see the same wax when it is before us, and not that we judge it to be the same from its retaining the same color and shape. From this I would be inclined at once to conclude that the wax is known by the act of sight, and not by the intuition of the mind alone — were it not for the parallel case of human beings passing in the street below, as observed from a window. In that case I do not fail to say that I see the men themselves, just as I say that I see the wax; and yet what do I see from the window beyond hats and cloaks that might be covering automata, whose movements might be controlled by springs? But I judge that there are human beings from these appearances, and so I grasp by the faculty of judgment alone, which is in the mind, what I believed I saw with my eyes.

14. The man who aims to rise to a knowledge superior to the ordinary should be ashamed to take occasions for doubt from common forms of speech. So instead of doing that, I will press on with the matter at hand, and inquire whether I had a clearer and more perfect perception of the piece of wax when I first saw it, and when I thought I knew it through the external sense itself — or, at any rate, through the common sense (sensus communis), as it is called, that is, through the imaginative faculty — or whether I rather grasp it more clearly now, after having examined more carefully both what it is and how it can be known. It would certainly be ridiculous to entertain any doubt on this point. For what was distinct in that first perception? What did I perceive that any animal might not have perceived? But when I distinguish the wax from its outer forms, and consider it, as it were, stripped of its garments and quite naked, it is certain — even though some error may still be found in my judgment — that I cannot apprehend it this way without having a human mind.

15. But finally, what shall I say of the mind itself — that is, of myself? For so far I do not admit that I am anything but mind. What, then! I, who seem to have so distinct an apprehension of the piece of wax, do I not know myself with even greater truth and certitude, and much more distinctly and clearly? For if I judge that the wax exists because I see it, surely it follows still more evidently that I myself am, or exist, for the same reason. It is possible that what I see is not really wax, and that I do not even have eyes with which to see anything; but it cannot be that, when I see — or, what comes to the same thing, when I think I see — I myself, who think, am nothing. Likewise, if I judge that the wax exists because I touch it, the same conclusion will follow — that I am. And if I determine that my imagination, or any other cause, persuades me of the wax's existence, I will still draw the same conclusion. What is observed here of the piece of wax applies to all the other things outside me. Furthermore, if the [notion or] perception of the wax appeared more precise and distinct to me after not only sight and touch, but many other causes besides, made it manifest to my apprehension, with how much greater distinctness must I now know myself, since all the reasons that contribute to the knowledge of the nature of the wax, or of any body whatever, reveal even better the nature of my mind? And there are besides so many other things in the mind itself that contribute to clarifying its nature, that what depends on the body, to which I have just referred, scarcely deserves to be taken into account.

16. But to conclude: I find that I have insensibly returned to the point I aimed at. For now that it is clear to me that bodies themselves are not properly perceived by the senses or by the faculty of imagination, but by the intellect alone — and that they are not perceived because they are seen and touched, but only because they are understood [or rightly comprehended by thought] — I readily see that there is nothing more easily or more clearly grasped than my own mind. But because it is difficult to break so quickly from an opinion to which one has long been accustomed, it will be best to linger here for a while, so that, by long-continued meditation, I may impress this new knowledge more deeply on my memory.

chapters.title: Meditation III — Of God: That He Exists
paragraphs: 1. I will now close my eyes, I will stop my ears, I will turn my senses away from their objects, I will even erase from my consciousness all the images of corporeal things — or, since this can hardly be done, I will at least consider them as empty and false. Holding converse only with myself, and closely examining my nature, I will try by degrees to gain a more intimate and familiar knowledge of myself. I am a thinking (conscious) thing — that is, a being who doubts, affirms, denies, knows a few objects and is ignorant of many, [who loves, hates,] wills, refuses, who imagines too, and perceives. For, as I noted before, although the things I perceive or imagine may be nothing at all apart from me [and in themselves], I am nevertheless sure that those modes of consciousness which I call perceptions and imaginations, insofar as they are merely modes of consciousness, do exist in me.

2. And in this little I have said I think I have summed up all that I really know — or at least all that, up to now, I was aware of knowing. Now, as I am trying to extend my knowledge further, I will use circumspection, and consider carefully whether I can still discover in myself anything I have not yet observed. I am certain that I am a thinking thing; but do I not therefore also know what is required to make me certain of a truth? In this first piece of knowledge there is nothing that gives me assurance of its truth except the clear and distinct perception of what I affirm — which would not in fact be enough to give me assurance that what I say is true, if it could ever happen that anything I clearly and distinctly perceived turned out to be false. Accordingly it seems to me that I may now take as a general rule: everything that is very clearly and distinctly apprehended (conceived) is true.

3. Yet I have previously received and admitted many things as wholly certain and manifest which I afterward found to be doubtful. What, then, were those? They were the earth, the sky, the stars, and all the other objects I was in the habit of perceiving by the senses. But what was it that I clearly [and distinctly] perceived in them? Nothing more than that ideas and thoughts of those objects were presented to my mind. Even now I do not deny that these ideas are found in my mind. But there was yet another thing I was affirming, which, from being in the habit of believing it, I thought I clearly perceived, although in truth I did not perceive it at all: I mean the existence of objects external to me, from which those ideas proceeded, and to which they were perfectly similar. It was here that I went wrong; or, if I happened to judge correctly, it was certainly not because of any knowledge I possessed (the force of my perception, Lat.).

4. But when I considered some matter in arithmetic and geometry that was very simple and easy — for example, that two and three added together make five, and things of that kind — did I not see them with at least enough clarity to warrant me in affirming their truth? Indeed, if I afterward judged that we ought to doubt these things, it was for no other reason than this: it occurred to me that God might perhaps have given me such a nature that I would be deceived even in matters that appeared to me most evidently true. But every time this preconceived opinion of God's sovereign power presents itself to my mind, I am forced to admit that it is easy for him, if he wishes, to make me err even in matters where I think I have the highest evidence. On the other hand, every time I direct my attention to things I think I apprehend with great clarity, I am so persuaded of their truth that I naturally break out into expressions like these: 'Let whoever can deceive me do so; he will never be able to bring it about that I am not, so long as I am conscious that I am'; or to make it true at any future time that I have never been, given that it is now true that I am; or to make two and three more or less than five — for in supposing such things and other like absurdities I find a manifest contradiction. And in truth, since I have no ground for believing that the Deity is deceitful, and since I have not yet even considered the reasons by which the existence of any kind of Deity is established, the ground for doubt that rests on this supposition alone is very slight, and, so to speak, metaphysical. To remove it entirely, I must inquire whether there is a God, as soon as the opportunity presents itself; and if I find that there is a God, I must also examine whether he can be a deceiver. For without the knowledge of these two truths I do not see how I can ever be certain of anything. So that I may examine this without breaking the order of meditation I have set for myself [namely, to pass by degrees from the notions I find first in my mind to those I shall afterward discover in it], it is necessary at this point to divide all my thoughts into certain classes, and to consider in which of these classes truth and error, strictly speaking, are to be found.

5. Some of my thoughts are, as it were, images of things, and to these alone properly belongs the name IDEA — as when I think [represent to my mind] a man, a chimera, the sky, an angel, or God. Others have additional forms; for when I will, fear, affirm, or deny, I always indeed grasp something as the object of my thought, but I also include in thought something more than the representation of the object. Of this class of thoughts, some are called volitions or affections, and others judgments.

6. Now, with respect to ideas, if they are considered only in themselves, and not referred to any object beyond them, they cannot, properly speaking, be false. For whether I imagine a goat or a chimera, it is no less true that I imagine the one than the other. Nor need we fear that falsity may be found in the will or affections; for although I may desire objects that are wrong, and even objects that never existed, it is still true that I desire them. There thus remain only our judgments, in which we must take diligent care not to be deceived. The chief and most ordinary error that arises in them consists in judging that the ideas which are in us are like, or conform to, things outside us. For surely, if we considered the ideas themselves merely as certain modes of our thought (consciousness), without referring them to anything beyond, they would hardly afford any occasion of error.

7. But among these ideas, some appear to me innate, others adventitious, and others made by myself (factitious). For since I have the power of conceiving what is called a thing, or a truth, or a thought, it seems to me that I hold this power from no source other than my own nature; but if I now hear a noise, or see the sun, or feel heat, I have all along judged that these sensations proceeded from certain objects existing outside me; and finally, it appears to me that sirens, hippogryphs, and the like are inventions of my own mind. But I may even come to think that all my ideas belong to the class I call adventitious, or that they are all innate, or that they are all factitious — for I have not yet clearly discovered their true origin.

8. What I have here principally to do is consider, with respect to those that appear to come from certain objects outside me, what grounds there are for thinking them similar to those objects. The first of these grounds is that it seems to me I am so taught by nature; the second is that I am conscious that those ideas do not depend on my will, and therefore not on me, since they are frequently presented to me against my will — as right now, whether I will it or not, I feel heat. I am thus persuaded that this sensation or idea (sensum vel ideam) of heat is produced in me by something different from myself, namely, by the heat of the fire I sit beside. And it is very reasonable to suppose that this object impresses me with its own likeness rather than with anything else.

9. But I must consider whether these reasons are sufficiently strong and convincing. When I speak of being taught by nature in this matter, I understand by the word nature only a certain spontaneous impulse that drives me to believe in a resemblance between ideas and their objects, and not a natural light that gives knowledge of its truth. These two things are widely different. What the natural light shows to be true cannot in any way be doubtful — for example, that I am because I doubt, and other truths of that kind — since I possess no other faculty for distinguishing truth from error that could teach me the falsity of what the natural light declares to be true and is equally trustworthy. But with respect to [seemingly] natural impulses, I have observed, when the question concerned the choice of right or wrong in action, that they often led me to take the worse part; and I see no better ground for following them in matters of truth and error.

10. Then, with respect to the other reason — that because these ideas do not depend on my will, they must arise from objects existing outside me — I do not find it any more convincing than the former. For just as those natural impulses I have just spoken of are found in me even though they are not always in agreement with my will, so likewise it may be that I possess some power, not sufficiently known to myself, capable of producing ideas without the aid of external objects. Indeed, it has always so far appeared to me that ideas are formed during sleep by some power of this kind, without the aid of anything external.

11. And finally, even if I should grant that they proceed from those objects, it is not a necessary consequence that they must resemble them. On the contrary, I have observed in many instances a great difference between an object and its idea. For example, I find in my mind two wholly diverse ideas of the sun. The one, by which it appears to me extremely small, draws its origin from the senses, and should be placed in the class of adventitious ideas. The other, by which it appears many times larger than the whole earth, is taken from astronomical grounds — that is, drawn from certain notions born with me, or framed by myself in some other way. These two ideas certainly cannot both resemble the same sun; and reason teaches me that the one which seems to have come immediately from it is the most unlike it.

12. These things are enough to show that, up to now, it has not been from a certain and deliberate judgment, but only from a kind of blind impulse, that I believed in the existence of certain things different from myself which, by the organs of sense, or by whatever other means, conveyed their ideas or images into my mind [and impressed it with their likenesses].

13. But there is still another way of inquiring whether, of the objects whose ideas are in my mind, there are any that exist outside me. If ideas are taken only insofar as they are certain modes of consciousness, I notice no difference or inequality among them — they all seem in the same way to proceed from myself. But considering them as images, of which one represents one thing and another a different thing, it is evident that a great diversity exists among them. For without doubt, those that represent substances are something more, and contain in themselves, so to speak, more objective reality [that is, participate by representation in higher degrees of being or perfection], than those that represent only modes or accidents. And again, the idea by which I conceive a God [sovereign], eternal, infinite, [immutable], all-knowing, all-powerful, and the creator of all things outside himself — this idea, I say, certainly contains in itself more objective reality than those by which finite substances are represented.

14. Now, it is manifest by the natural light that there must be at least as much reality in the efficient and total cause as in its effect. For from where could the effect draw its reality, if not from its cause? And how could the cause communicate this reality to it, unless it possessed it in itself? From this it follows not only that what is cannot be produced by what is not, but also that the more perfect — that is, what contains in itself more reality — cannot be the effect of the less perfect. And this is plainly true not only of those effects whose reality is actual or formal, but also of ideas, whose reality is considered only as objective. So, for example, the stone that does not yet exist not only cannot now begin to be unless it is produced by something that possesses in itself, formally or eminently, all that enters into its composition [that is, by something that contains in itself the same properties that are in the stone, or others superior to them]; and heat can be produced in a subject previously without it only by a cause of an order, [degree or kind,] at least as perfect as heat; and so on. But further, even the idea of heat, or of the stone, cannot exist in me unless it has been put there by a cause that contains at least as much reality as I conceive to exist in the heat or in the stone. For although that cause may not transfer to my idea anything of its actual or formal reality, we ought not on this account to imagine that the idea is less real. Rather we should consider that [as every idea is a work of the mind], its nature is such as to demand of itself no other formal reality than what it borrows from our consciousness, of which it is only a mode [that is, a manner or way of thinking]. But in order for an idea to contain this objective reality rather than that, it must surely derive it from some cause in which is found at least as much formal reality as the idea contains of objective reality. For if we suppose that there is something found in an idea which was not in its cause, then it must derive this from nothing. But however imperfect the mode of existence by which a thing is objectively [or by representation] in the understanding through its idea, we still cannot say that this mode of existence is nothing, nor, consequently, that the idea owes its origin to nothing.

15. Nor should it be imagined that, since the reality considered in these ideas is only objective, that same reality need not exist formally (actually) in their causes, but only objectively. For just as the mode of existing objectively belongs to ideas by their peculiar nature, so likewise the mode of existing formally belongs to the causes of these ideas (at least to the first and principal causes) by their peculiar nature. And although one idea may give rise to another, this regress cannot be infinite. We must in the end reach a first idea, the cause of which is, as it were, the archetype in which all the reality [or perfection] that is found objectively [or by representation] in these ideas is contained formally [and in act]. The natural light thus clearly teaches me that ideas exist in me as pictures or images that may, in truth, readily fall short of the perfection of the objects from which they are drawn, but can never contain anything greater or more perfect.

16. And in proportion to the time and care with which I examine all these matters, the conviction of their truth grows brighter and becomes distinct. But, to sum up: what conclusion shall I draw from all this? It is this: if the objective reality [or perfection] of any one of my ideas is such as to convince me clearly that this same reality exists in me neither formally nor eminently, and that, as follows from this, I myself cannot be the cause of it, then it follows necessarily that I am not alone in the world, but that there is, besides me, some other being who exists as the cause of that idea. On the contrary, if no such idea is found in my mind, I shall have no sufficient ground for assurance that any other being besides me exists; for, after the most careful search, I have so far been unable to discover any other.

17. But among my ideas, besides the one that represents myself — about which there can be no difficulty here — there is one that represents a God; others that represent corporeal and inanimate things; others, angels; others, animals; and finally, some that represent men like myself.

18. With respect to the ideas that represent other men, or animals, or angels, I can easily suppose that they were formed by the mingling and composition of the other ideas I have of myself, of corporeal things, and of God — even if, apart from me, there were no men, animals, or angels at all.

19. And with regard to the ideas of corporeal objects, I never discovered in them anything so great or excellent that I did not appear capable of originating it myself. For by considering these ideas closely and scrutinizing them one by one, in the same way I yesterday examined the idea of wax, I find that there is little in them that is clearly and distinctly perceived. As belonging to the class of things clearly apprehended, I recognize the following: magnitude or extension in length, breadth, and depth; shape, which results from the termination of extension; situation, which bodies of diverse shapes preserve with respect to one another; and motion, or change of situation — to which may be added substance, duration, and number. But with regard to light, colors, sounds, odors, tastes, heat, cold, and the other tactile qualities, these are thought with such obscurity and confusion that I cannot even determine whether they are true or false — that is, whether the ideas I have of these qualities are in truth ideas of real objects or not. Although I noted earlier that formal falsity, or falsity properly so called, can be met with only in judgments, there may nevertheless be found in ideas a certain material falsity, which arises when they represent what is nothing as if it were something. Thus, for example, my ideas of cold and heat are so far from being clear and distinct that I cannot tell from them whether cold is only the privation of heat, or heat the privation of cold; or whether they are or are not real qualities. And since ideas are, as it were, images, there can be none that does not seem to us to represent some object. The idea that represents cold as something real and positive will not improperly be called false, if it is correct to say that cold is nothing but a privation of heat; and so on in other cases.

20. To ideas of this kind, indeed, I need assign no author besides myself. For if they are false — that is, if they represent objects that are unreal — the natural light teaches me that they proceed from nothing; in other words, that they are in me only because something is lacking in the perfection of my nature. But if these ideas are true, then because they exhibit to me so little reality that I cannot even distinguish the object represented from non-being, I do not see why I should not be the author of them.

21. As for those ideas of corporeal things that are clear and distinct, some, it seems to me, might have been taken from the idea I have of myself — such as the ideas of substance, duration, number, and the like. For when I think that a stone is a substance, or a thing capable of existing of itself, and that I likewise am a substance, even though I conceive that I am a thinking, non-extended thing while the stone, on the contrary, is extended and unconscious — so that the greatest diversity exists between the two concepts — these two ideas still seem to have this in common: they both represent substances. In the same way, when I think of myself as now existing, and remember that I existed some time ago, and when I am conscious of various thoughts whose number I know, I then acquire the ideas of duration and number, which I can afterward transfer to as many objects as I please. With respect to the other qualities that go to make up the ideas of corporeal objects — namely, extension, shape, situation, and motion — it is true that they are not formally in me, since I am merely a thinking being. But because they are only certain modes of substance, and because I am myself a substance, it seems possible that they may be contained in me eminently.

22. There remains, therefore, only the idea of God, in which I must consider whether there is anything that cannot be supposed to originate with myself. By the name God, I understand a substance that is infinite, [eternal, immutable,] independent, all-knowing, all-powerful, and by which I myself, and every other thing that exists (if any other does), were created. But these properties are so great and excellent that the more attentively I consider them, the less I feel persuaded that the idea I have of them owes its origin to me alone. So it is absolutely necessary to conclude, from all I have said before, that God exists.

23. For though the idea of substance is in my mind because I am myself a substance, I would not have the idea of an infinite substance — being a finite being — unless it were given me by some substance really infinite.

24. And I must not imagine that I do not apprehend the infinite by a true idea, but only by negation of the finite, in the same way that I grasp rest and darkness by the negation of motion and light. On the contrary, I clearly perceive that there is more reality in the infinite substance than in the finite, and therefore that in some way I possess the perception (notion) of the infinite before that of the finite — that is, the perception of God before that of myself. For how could I know that I doubt, or desire, or that something is wanting in me, and that I am not wholly perfect, if I had no idea of a being more perfect than myself, by comparison with which I recognize the deficiencies of my nature?

25. And it cannot be said that this idea of God is perhaps materially false, and consequently that it may have arisen from nothing [in other words, that it may exist in me from my imperfections, as I said before of the ideas of heat and cold and the like]. On the contrary, since this idea is very clear and distinct, and contains in itself more objective reality than any other, there can be no idea more true in itself, or less open to the suspicion of falsity. The idea, I say, of a being supremely perfect and infinite is in the highest degree true. For although we may perhaps imagine that such a being does not exist, we cannot suppose that his idea represents nothing real, as I have already said of the idea of cold. It is also clear and distinct in the highest degree, since whatever the mind clearly and distinctly conceives as real or true, and as implying any perfection, is contained entire in this idea. And this is true even though I do not comprehend the infinite, and although there may be in God an infinity of things that I cannot comprehend, nor perhaps even reach by thought in any way; for it is of the nature of the infinite that it should not be comprehended by the finite. It is enough that I rightly understand this, and judge that everything I clearly perceive, and in which I know there is some perfection — and perhaps also an infinity of properties of which I am ignorant — is formally or eminently in God, in order that the idea I have of him may become the most true, clear, and distinct of all the ideas in my mind.

26. But perhaps I am something more than I take myself to be, and perhaps all those perfections I attribute to God exist potentially in me in some way, although they do not yet show themselves and are not reduced to act. Indeed, I am already aware that my knowledge is being increased [and perfected] by degrees; and I see nothing to prevent it from gradually increasing to infinity, nor any reason why, after such increase and perfection, I should not be able by it to acquire all the other perfections of the Divine nature; nor, finally, why the power I possess of acquiring those perfections, if it really now exists in me, should not be sufficient to produce the ideas of them.

27. Yet on looking more closely into the matter, I see that this cannot be. In the first place, even if it were true that my knowledge daily acquired new degrees of perfection, and that there were potentially in my nature much that was not yet actually in it, all these excellences make not the slightest approach to the idea I have of the Deity, in whom no perfection exists merely potentially [but all actually]. It is even an unmistakable token of imperfection in my knowledge that it is augmented by degrees. Further, although my knowledge increase more and more, I am not therefore led to think that it will ever be actually infinite, since it can never reach the point beyond which it would be incapable of further increase. But I conceive God as actually infinite, so that nothing can be added to his perfection. And finally, I readily perceive that the objective being of an idea cannot be produced by a being that is merely potentially existent — which, properly speaking, is nothing — but only by a being existing formally or actually.

28. And, truly, I see nothing in all I have just said that anyone who carefully considers it may not easily discern by the natural light.
