But when I let my attention slacken even a little — my mind's vision being obscured and, as it were, blinded by images of sensible objects — I do not readily remember the reason why the idea of a being more perfect than myself must necessarily have proceeded from a being in reality more perfect. For this reason I want to inquire further here whether I, who possess this idea of God, could exist if there were no God.

29. And from whom, in that case, could I derive my existence? Perhaps from myself, or from my parents, or from some other causes less perfect than God — for nothing more perfect, or even equal to God, can be thought or imagined.

30. But if I [were independent of every other existence, and] were myself the author of my being, I would doubt nothing, I would desire nothing, and finally no perfection would be lacking in me. For I would have bestowed on myself every perfection of which I have the idea, and I would thus be God. Nor must it be imagined that what I now lack might be more difficult to acquire than what I already possess. On the contrary, it is quite plain that it was a matter of much higher difficulty that I, a thinking being, should arise from nothing, than it would be for me to acquire the knowledge of many things of which I am ignorant — things which are merely the accidents of a thinking substance. Certainly, if I had given myself the greater perfection just spoken of [in other words, if I were the author of my own existence], I would not at least have denied to myself things more easily obtained [such as that infinite variety of knowledge of which I am at present destitute]. Nor could I have denied to myself any property I perceive to be contained in the idea of God, since none of these seems to me more difficult to make or to acquire than any other; and if there were any that did happen to be more difficult, they would surely appear so to me (supposing I were myself the source of the other things I possess), because I would discover in them a limit to my power.

31. And even if I were to suppose that I have always been as I now am, I would not on this ground escape the force of these arguments, since it would not follow, even on this supposition, that no author of my existence needs to be sought after. For the whole time of my life can be divided into an infinity of parts, each of which in no way depends on any other; and so, because I existed a short time ago, it does not follow that I must now exist, unless in this moment some cause creates me anew, as it were — that is, conserves me. In truth, it is perfectly clear and evident to all who attentively consider the nature of duration that the conservation of a substance, at each moment of its duration, requires the same power and act that would be needed to create it, supposing it did not yet exist. So that it is plainly a dictate of the natural light that conservation and creation differ only in our way of thinking [and not in reality].

32. All that is required here, therefore, is that I question myself to discover whether I possess any power by means of which I can bring it about that I, who now am, shall exist a moment afterward. For since I am merely a thinking thing (or, at any rate, since the precise question for the moment concerns only that part of myself), if such a power resided in me I would surely be conscious of it. But I am conscious of no such power, and from this I plainly know that I depend on some being other than myself.

33. But perhaps the being on whom I depend is not God, and I have been produced either by my parents, or by some causes less perfect than the Deity. This cannot be. For, as I said before, it is perfectly evident that there must be at least as much reality in the cause as in its effect. Accordingly, since I am a thinking thing and possess in myself an idea of God, whatever the cause of my existence ultimately is, it must necessarily be admitted that it is likewise a thinking being, and that it possesses in itself the idea and all the perfections I attribute to the Deity. Then it may again be inquired whether this cause owes its origin and existence to itself, or to some other cause. If it is self-existent, it follows from what I have already laid down that this cause is God: for since it possesses the perfection of self-existence, it must also, without doubt, have the power of actually possessing every perfection of which it has the idea — in other words, all the perfections I conceive to belong to God. But if it owes its existence to another cause than itself, we ask again, for the same reason, whether this second cause exists of itself or through some other — until, from stage to stage, we at last arrive at an ultimate cause, which will be God.

34. And it is quite plain that in this matter there can be no infinite regress of causes, since the question raised concerns not so much the cause that once produced me as the cause by which I am at this present moment conserved.

35. Nor can it be supposed that several causes concurred in my production — that from one I received the idea of one of the perfections I attribute to the Deity, and from another the idea of another, so that all these perfections are indeed found somewhere in the universe, but do not all exist together in a single being who is God. On the contrary, the unity, simplicity, or inseparability of all the properties of the Deity is one of the chief perfections I conceive him to possess; and the idea of this unity of all the perfections of the Deity certainly could not have been put into my mind by any cause from which I did not also receive the ideas of all the other perfections. For no power could enable me to grasp them in an inseparable unity, without at the same time giving me the knowledge of what they were [and of their existence in a particular mode].

36. Finally, with regard to my parents [from whom it appears I sprang], even though everything I believed about them is true, it still does not follow that I am conserved by them, or even that I was produced by them insofar as I am a thinking being. At most, all they contributed to my origin was the giving of certain dispositions (modifications) to the matter in which I have so far judged that I, or my mind — which alone I now consider to be myself — is enclosed. So there can be no difficulty with respect to them here. And it is absolutely necessary to conclude from this alone — that I am, and possess the idea of a being absolutely perfect, that is, of God — that his existence is most clearly demonstrated.

37. There remains only the inquiry into how I received this idea from God. For I have not drawn it from the senses, nor is it even presented to me unexpectedly, as is usual with the ideas of sensible objects, when these are presented or appear to be presented to the external organs of the senses; nor is it a pure production or fiction of my mind, for it is not in my power to take from it or add to it. Consequently, the only remaining alternative is that it is innate, in the same way as the idea of myself.

38. And in truth it is not to be wondered at that God, at my creation, implanted this idea in me, that it might serve, as it were, for the mark of the workman impressed on his work; and it is not necessary that the mark should be something different from the work itself. Considering only that God is my creator, it is highly probable that he in some way fashioned me after his own image and likeness, and that I perceive this likeness — in which is contained the idea of God — by the same faculty by which I apprehend myself. In other words, when I make myself the object of reflection, I not only find that I am an incomplete, [imperfect,] and dependent being, one who unceasingly aspires after something better and greater than he is; but I am also assured that he on whom I depend possesses in himself all the goods after which I aspire [and the ideas of which I find in my mind], and possesses them not merely indefinitely and potentially, but infinitely and actually, and is thus God. And the whole force of the argument I have here used to establish the existence of God consists in this: I perceive that I could not possibly be of such a nature as I am, and yet have in my mind the idea of a God, if God did not in reality exist — the same God, I say, whose idea is in my mind — that is, a being who possesses all those lofty perfections of which my mind may have some slight conception (without being able fully to comprehend them), and who is wholly superior to all defect [and has nothing that marks imperfection]. From this it is sufficiently plain that he cannot be a deceiver, since it is a dictate of the natural light that all fraud and deception spring from some defect.

39. But before I examine this with more attention, and pass on to the consideration of other truths that may be developed out of it, I think it proper to remain here for some time in the contemplation of God himself — to ponder at leisure his marvelous attributes, and to behold, admire, and adore the beauty of this light so unspeakably great, at least as far as the strength of my mind, which is to some degree dazzled by the sight, will permit. For just as we learn by faith that the supreme felicity of another life consists in the contemplation of the Divine majesty alone, so even now we learn from experience that a like meditation, though incomparably less perfect, is the source of the highest satisfaction we are capable of in this life.

chapters.title: Meditation IV — Of Truth and Error
paragraphs: 1. I have grown used during these past days to detaching my mind from the senses, and I have observed precisely how very little can be known with certainty about corporeal objects, how much more we know of the human mind, and still more of God himself. I am thus able now, without difficulty, to abstract my mind from the contemplation of [sensible or] imaginable things, and to apply it to those that, being disengaged from all matter, are purely intelligible. And certainly the idea I have of the human mind insofar as it is a thinking thing — not extended in length, breadth, or depth, and sharing none of the properties of body — is incomparably more distinct than the idea of any corporeal object. When I consider that I doubt — that I am, in other words, an incomplete and dependent being — the idea of a complete and independent being, that is, of God, occurs to my mind with so much clearness and distinctness, that from the mere fact this idea is found in me (or that I, who possess it, exist), the conclusions that God exists, and that my own existence depends absolutely on him at every moment of its continuance, are so manifest that I cannot believe the human mind capable of knowing anything with greater clarity and certitude. And now I seem to discover a path that will lead from the contemplation of the true God — in whom are contained all the treasures of science and wisdom — to the knowledge of the other things in the universe.

2. For in the first place, I see that it is impossible for him ever to deceive me, since in all fraud and deceit there is a certain imperfection. Although the ability to deceive may seem a mark of subtlety or power, the will to deceive bears witness, without doubt, to malice and weakness; and such cannot be found in God.

3. Next, I am conscious that I possess a certain faculty of judging [or discerning truth from error], which I doubtless received from God, along with whatever else is mine; and since it is impossible that he should will to deceive me, it is likewise certain that he has not given me a faculty that will ever lead me into error, provided I use it rightly.

4. There would remain no doubt on this point, did it not seem to follow that I can therefore never be deceived. For if all I possess comes from God, and if he planted in me no faculty that is deceitful, it seems to follow that I can never fall into error. Accordingly, when I think only of God (when I look upon myself as coming from God, Fr.), and turn wholly to him, I find [in myself] no cause of error or falsity; but as soon as I turn back to myself, experience assures me that I am nevertheless subject to innumerable errors. When I look into the cause of these, I observe that there is present to my consciousness not only a real and positive idea of God, or of a supremely perfect being, but also, so to speak, a certain negative idea of nothing — that is, of what is at an infinite distance from every kind of perfection. I am, as it were, a mean between God and nothing, placed in such a way between absolute existence and non-existence that, in truth, there is in me nothing to lead me into error insofar as an absolute being is my creator; but on the other hand, since I likewise share in some degree of nothingness, or non-being — that is, since I am not myself the supreme Being, and lack many perfections — it is not surprising that I should fall into error. From this I see that error, insofar as it is error, is not something real that depends for its existence on God, but is simply a defect; and therefore that, in order for me to fall into it, God did not need to have given me a faculty expressly for this end. My being deceived arises from the fact that the power God has given me of discerning truth from error is not infinite.

5. Yet this is still not quite satisfactory; for error is not a pure negation [in other words, it is not the simple absence of some knowledge that is not due], but the privation, or want, of some knowledge that I would seem to ought to possess. But considering the nature of God, it seems impossible that he should have planted in his creature any faculty not perfect in its kind — that is, lacking some perfection due to it. For if it is true that the more skillful the maker, the greater the perfection of his work, what could the supreme Creator of the universe have produced that is not absolutely perfect in all its parts? And surely there is no doubt that God could have created me such that I should never be deceived; it is also certain that he always wills what is best. Is it better, then, that I should be capable of being deceived than that I should not?

6. Considering this more attentively, the first thing that occurs to me is that I should not be surprised if I am not always able to comprehend the reasons why God acts as he does; nor must I doubt his existence because I find, perhaps, that there are several other things, besides the present one, of which I understand neither why nor how they were created by him. For knowing already that my nature is extremely weak and limited, and that the nature of God, on the other hand, is immense, incomprehensible, and infinite, I no longer have any difficulty in seeing that there is an infinity of things in his power whose causes transcend the grasp of my mind. This consideration alone is enough to convince me that the whole class of final causes is of no avail in physical [or natural] things; for it appears to me that I cannot, without exposing myself to a charge of presumption, seek to discover the [impenetrable] ends of the Deity.

7. It further occurs to me that we must not consider only one creature in isolation from the others if we wish to determine the perfection of God's works, but generally all his creatures together. For the very same object that might perhaps, with some show of reason, be called highly imperfect if it were alone in the world, may nevertheless be the most perfect thing possible considered as a part of the whole universe. And although, since it was my purpose to doubt of everything, I as yet know with certainty only my own existence and that of God, still, having noted the infinite power of the Deity, I cannot deny that he may have produced many other objects, or at least is able to produce them — so that I may occupy a place in the relation of a part to the great whole of his creatures.

8. Whereupon, looking at myself more closely and considering what my errors are (which alone testify to imperfection in me), I observe that they depend on the concurrence of two causes: the faculty of cognition, which I possess, and the faculty of election, or the power of free choice — in other words, the understanding and the will. For by the understanding alone I [neither affirm nor deny anything, but] merely apprehend (percipio) the ideas about which I may form a judgment; nor is any error, properly so called, found in it thus precisely taken. And although there are perhaps innumerable objects in the world of which I have no idea in my understanding, it cannot on that account be said that I am deprived of those ideas [as of something due to my nature], but simply that I do not possess them. For there is no reason to prove that the Deity ought to have endowed me with a larger faculty of cognition than the one he has actually given me; and however skillful a workman I suppose him to be, I have no reason to think that he was obliged to give to each of his works all the perfections he is able to bestow on some. Nor, moreover, can I complain that God has not given me freedom of choice, or a will sufficiently ample and perfect, since in truth I am conscious of a will so ample and extensive that it is superior to all limits. And what appears to me here highly remarkable is that, of all the other properties I possess, there is none so great and perfect that I do not clearly see it could be still greater and more perfect. For example, if I consider the faculty of understanding I possess, I find that it is of very small extent and greatly limited; and at the same time I form the idea of another faculty of the same kind, much more ample, and even infinite. Seeing that I can frame the idea of it, I see from this circumstance alone that it pertains to the nature of God. In the same way, if I examine the faculty of memory, or imagination, or any other faculty I possess, I find none that is not small and circumscribed, and in God immense [and infinite]. It is the faculty of will alone, or freedom of choice, which I experience to be so great that I am unable to conceive the idea of any greater and more extensive will. So that it is chiefly my will which leads me to see that I bear a certain image and likeness of the Deity. For although the faculty of will is incomparably greater in God than in me — both with respect to the knowledge and power conjoined with it (which make it stronger and more efficacious), and with respect to its object, since in him it extends to a greater number of things — it does not, considered in itself, formally and precisely, appear to me greater. The power of will consists only in this, that we are able to do or not to do the same thing (that is, to affirm or deny, to pursue or shun it); or rather, in this alone, that in affirming or denying, pursuing or shunning what is proposed to us by the understanding, we so act that we are not conscious of being determined to a particular action by any external force. For freedom does not require that I be equally indifferent toward each of two contraries; on the contrary, the more I am inclined toward one — whether because I clearly know that in it lies the reason of truth and goodness, or because God thus inwardly disposes my thought — the more freely do I choose and embrace it. And surely divine grace and natural knowledge, far from diminishing liberty, augment and fortify it. But the indifference I am conscious of when I am not impelled to one side rather than the other for want of a reason is the lowest grade of liberty, and shows defect or want of knowledge rather than perfection of will. For if I always clearly knew what was true and good, I would never have any difficulty in determining what judgment to come to, and what choice to make; and I would thus be entirely free, without ever being indifferent.

9. From all this I see, however, that neither the power of willing, which I have received from God, is of itself the source of my errors — for it is exceedingly ample and perfect of its kind — nor is even the power of understanding. For since I conceive no object except by means of the faculty God bestowed on me, all that I conceive is doubtless rightly conceived by me, and it is impossible for me to be deceived in it. Where, then, do my errors spring from? They arise from this cause alone: that I do not restrain the will, which is of much wider range than the understanding, within the same limits, but extend it even to things I do not understand. And since the will is of itself indifferent to such things, it readily falls into error and sin by choosing the false in place of the true, and evil in place of good.

10. For example, when I considered, just now, whether anything really existed in the world, and found that, because I considered this question, it very plainly followed that I myself existed, I could not but judge that what I so clearly conceived was true — not because I was forced to this judgment by any external cause, but simply because great clearness of the understanding was followed by strong inclination in the will; and I believed it the more freely and spontaneously the less indifferent I was about it. But now I not only know that I exist, insofar as I am a thinking being, but there is also presented to my mind a certain idea of corporeal nature; so I am in doubt whether the thinking nature in me — or rather, that which I myself am — is different from that corporeal nature, or whether both are merely one and the same thing. And I here suppose that I am as yet ignorant of any reason that would lead me to adopt one belief in preference to the other; whence it happens that it is a matter of perfect indifference to me which of the two suppositions I affirm or deny, or whether I form any judgment at all on the matter.

11. This indifference, moreover, extends not only to things of which the understanding has no knowledge at all, but generally also to all those things it does not discover with perfect clearness at the moment the will is deliberating on them. For however probable the conjectures may be that incline me to form a judgment on a particular matter, the mere knowledge that these are conjectures only, and not certain and indubitable reasons, is enough to lead me to form the directly opposite judgment. Of this I had abundant experience just lately, when I laid aside as false everything I had previously held for true, on the single ground that I could in some degree doubt it.

12. But if I abstain from judging a thing when I do not conceive it with sufficient clearness and distinctness, it is plain that I act rightly and am not deceived; whereas if I resolve to deny or affirm, I then do not make a right use of my free will. And if I affirm what is false, it is plain that I am deceived; and even if I judge according to truth, I stumble on it by chance, and do not therefore escape the charge of misusing my freedom. For it is a dictate of the natural light that the knowledge of the understanding ought always to precede the determination of the will. It is in this wrong use of the freedom of the will that the privation lies which constitutes the form of error. Privation, I say, is found in the act insofar as it proceeds from myself; but it does not exist in the faculty I received from God, nor even in the act insofar as it depends on him.

13. For I have surely no reason to complain that God has not given me a greater power of intelligence, or a more perfect natural light, than he has actually bestowed; since it is in the nature of a finite understanding not to comprehend many things, and in the nature of a created understanding to be finite. On the contrary, I have every reason to give thanks to God, who owed me nothing, for having given me all the perfections I possess; and I should be far from thinking that he has unjustly deprived me of, or withheld, the other perfections he has not bestowed on me.

14. I have no reason, moreover, to complain that he has given me a will more ample than my understanding; for since the will consists only of a single element, and that indivisible, it appears that this faculty is of such a nature that nothing could be taken from it [without destroying it]. And certainly, the more extensive it is, the more cause I have to thank the goodness of him who bestowed it on me.

15. And finally, I ought not even to complain that God concurs with me in forming the acts of this will, or the judgments in which I am deceived; because those acts are wholly true and good, insofar as they depend on God, and the ability to form them is a higher degree of perfection in my nature than the want of it would be. With regard to privation — in which alone consists the formal reason of error and sin — this does not require the concurrence of the Deity, because it is not a thing [or existence]; and if it is referred to God as to its cause, it ought not to be called privation, but negation [according to the signification of these words in the schools]. For in truth it is no imperfection in the Deity that he has granted me the power of giving or withholding my assent from certain things of which he has not put a clear and distinct knowledge in my understanding; but it is doubtless an imperfection in me that I do not use my freedom rightly, and readily pass judgment on matters that I only obscurely and confusedly conceive. I perceive, nevertheless, that it would have been easy for the Deity so to have constituted me that I should never be deceived, although I remained free and possessed of a limited knowledge — namely, by implanting in my understanding a clear and distinct knowledge of all the objects on which I should ever have to deliberate; or simply by so deeply engraving on my memory the resolution to judge of nothing without first having a clear and distinct conception of it, that I should never forget it. And I easily understand that, considering myself as a single whole, without reference to any other being in the universe, I should have been much more perfect than I now am, had the Deity created me superior to error. But I cannot therefore deny that it is somehow a greater perfection in the universe that some of its parts are not exempt from defect, as others are, than if they were all perfectly alike. And I have no right to complain because God, who placed me in the world, was not willing that I should bear the character which, of all others, is the chief and most perfect.

16. I have even good reason to remain satisfied on the ground that, if he has not given me the perfection of being superior to error by the first means I pointed out above — which depends on a clear and evident knowledge of all the matters about which I can deliberate — he has at least left in my power the other means, namely, firmly to hold to the resolution never to judge where the truth is not clearly known to me. For although I am conscious of the weakness of not being able to keep my mind continually fixed on the same thought, I can nevertheless, by attentive and often-repeated meditation, impress it so strongly on my memory that I shall never fail to recall it as often as I need it; and I can in this way acquire the habit of not erring.

17. And since the highest and chief perfection of man consists in being superior to error, I think I have gained no little by today's meditation in having discovered the source of error and falsity. And certainly this can be no other than what I have now explained. For whenever I so restrain my will within the limits of my knowledge that it forms no judgment except about objects clearly and distinctly represented to it by the understanding, I can never be deceived; because every clear and distinct conception is doubtless something, and as such cannot owe its origin to nothing, but must necessarily have God for its author — God, I say, who, as supremely perfect, cannot, without contradiction, be the cause of any error. So it is necessary to conclude that every such conception [or judgment] is true. Nor have I merely learned today what I must avoid in order to escape error, but also what I must do to arrive at the knowledge of truth: for I shall surely reach the truth if I fix my attention sufficiently on everything I conceive perfectly, and separate it from what I conceive more confusedly and obscurely. To this I shall give diligent heed from now on.

chapters.title: Meditation V — Of the Essence of Material Things; And, Again, Of God: That He Exists
paragraphs: 1. Several other questions remain to be considered concerning the attributes of God and my own nature, or mind. I will, however, perhaps take up the investigation of these on another occasion. Meanwhile, having discovered what must be done and what must be avoided to arrive at the knowledge of truth, what I now have chiefly to do is try to emerge from the state of doubt in which I have been for some time, and find out whether anything can be known with certainty about material objects.

2. But before considering whether such objects as I conceive exist outside me, I must examine the ideas of them insofar as these are found in my consciousness, and discover which are distinct and which confused.

3. In the first place, I distinctly imagine that quantity which philosophers commonly call continuous — the extension in length, breadth, and depth which is in this quantity, or rather in the object to which it is attributed. Further, I can enumerate within it many diverse parts, and assign to each of them all kinds of sizes, shapes, situations, and local motions; and finally, I can assign to each of these motions all degrees of duration.

4. And I not only know these things distinctly when I consider them in general; but with a little attention I also discover innumerable particulars about shapes, numbers, motion, and the like, which are so evidently true and so in accord with my nature that, when I now discover them, I do not so much seem to learn anything new as to recall what I knew before, or to notice for the first time what was already in my mind, but to which I had not yet directed my attention.

5. And what I find here of greatest importance is that I discover in my mind innumerable ideas of certain objects which cannot be regarded as pure negations, even though they may have no reality beyond my thought; ideas not framed by me — though it is in my power to think of them or not — but possessing true and immutable natures of their own. For example, when I imagine a triangle, even though no such figure perhaps exists, or ever existed, anywhere in the universe apart from my thought, this figure nevertheless possesses a certain determinate nature, form, or essence, which is immutable and eternal, not framed by me, and not in any way dependent on my thought. This is shown by the fact that diverse properties of the triangle can be demonstrated — that its three angles equal two right angles, that the longest side is opposite the largest angle, and the like — properties which, whether I will it or not, I now clearly see belong to it, even though I did not think of them at all when I first imagined a triangle, and which therefore cannot be said to have been invented by me.

6. Nor is it a valid objection to say that perhaps this idea of a triangle came into my mind through the senses, by my having seen bodies of triangular shape. For I can form in thought an innumerable variety of figures of which it cannot be supposed that they were ever objects of sense; and I can nevertheless demonstrate diverse properties of their nature no less than of the triangle — all of which are surely true since I clearly conceive them. They are therefore something, and not mere negations; for it is highly evident that all that is true is something [truth being identical with existence]. And I have already fully shown the truth of the principle that whatever is clearly and distinctly known is true. Even if this had not been demonstrated, the nature of my mind is such as to compel me to assent to what I clearly conceive while I so conceive it. And I recall that even when I still strongly clung to the objects of sense, I numbered among the most certain truths those I clearly conceived about figures, numbers, and other matters that pertain to arithmetic and geometry, and in general to the pure mathematics.

7. But now if, because I can draw from my thought the idea of an object, it follows that everything I clearly and distinctly apprehend to belong to this object does in truth belong to it — may I not derive from this an argument for the existence of God? It is certain that I find the idea of God in my consciousness — that is, the idea of a supremely perfect being — no less than the idea of any figure or number whatever; and I know with no less clearness and distinctness that an [actual and] eternal existence pertains to his nature than that everything demonstrable of any figure or number really belongs to the nature of that figure or number. And therefore, even if all the conclusions of the previous Meditations were false, the existence of God would still pass with me as a truth at least as certain as I ever judged any truth of mathematics to be.

8. At first sight, indeed, such a doctrine may appear to contain more sophistry than truth. For since I have been used in every other matter to distinguish between existence and essence, I easily believe that existence can be separated from the essence of God, and that God may thus be conceived as not actually existing. But when I think of it more carefully, it appears that existence can no more be separated from the essence of God than the idea of a mountain can be separated from that of a valley, or the equality of its three angles to two right angles from the essence of a [rectilinear] triangle. So that it is no less impossible to conceive a God — that is, a supremely perfect being — to whom existence is wanting, or who is devoid of a certain perfection, than to conceive a mountain without a valley.

9. But although in truth I cannot conceive a God except as existing, any more than I can conceive a mountain without a valley, it does not follow that there is any mountain in the world simply because I conceive a mountain with a valley; so likewise, although I conceive God as existing, it does not seem to follow on that account that God exists. For my thought imposes no necessity on things; and just as I may imagine a winged horse, though no such thing exists, so I might perhaps attribute existence to God even though no God existed.

10. But the cases are not analogous, and a fallacy lurks beneath the appearance of this objection. For from the fact that I cannot conceive a mountain without a valley, it does not follow that any mountain or valley actually exists, but only that mountain and valley, whether they exist or not, are inseparable from each other. Whereas, on the other hand, from the fact that I cannot conceive God except as existing, it follows that existence is inseparable from him, and therefore that he really exists. Not that this is brought about by my thought, or that my thought imposes any necessity on things; but, on the contrary, the necessity that lies in the thing itself — that is, the necessity of God's existence — determines me to think this way. For it is not in my power to conceive a God without existence — that is, a supremely perfect being yet devoid of an absolute perfection — as I am free to imagine a horse with or without wings.

11. Nor must it be objected here that, in truth, it is necessary to admit that God exists, having supposed him to possess all perfections (since existence is one of them), but that my original supposition was not necessary — just as it is not necessary to think that all quadrilateral figures can be inscribed in a circle, since, if I supposed this, I would be forced to admit that a rhombus, being a four-sided figure, could be inscribed in it, which is plainly false. This objection, I say, is not valid. For although it may not be necessary that I should ever entertain the notion of the Deity, yet whenever I happen to think of a first and sovereign being, and to draw, so to speak, the idea of him from the storehouse of my mind, I am necessitated to attribute to him all kinds of perfections, even if I do not then enumerate them all, or think of each of them in particular. And this necessity is enough, as soon as I see that existence is a perfection, to make me infer the existence of this first and sovereign being. Just as it is not necessary that I should ever imagine any triangle; but whenever I want to consider a rectilinear figure composed of only three angles, it is absolutely necessary to attribute to it those properties from which it is correctly inferred that its three angles are not greater than two right angles, even though I may not advert to this relation in particular. But when I consider what figures can be inscribed in a circle, it is by no means necessary to hold that all quadrilateral figures are among them; on the contrary, I cannot even imagine such to be the case, so long as I am unwilling to accept in thought anything that I do not clearly and distinctly conceive. Consequently there is a vast difference between false suppositions, such as the one in question, and the true ideas that were born with me — the first and chief of which is the idea of God. For I see on many grounds that this idea is not factitious, depending simply on my thought, but is the representation of a true and immutable nature. First, because I can conceive of no other being, except God, to whose essence existence [necessarily] belongs; second, because it is impossible to conceive two or more gods of this kind, and supposing that one such God exists, I clearly see that he must have existed from all eternity, and will exist to all eternity; and finally, because I apprehend many other properties in God, none of which I can either diminish or change.

12. But indeed, whatever mode of proof I in the end adopt, it always comes back to this: only the things I clearly and distinctly conceive have the power of completely persuading me. And although, among the objects I conceive this way, some are obvious to everyone, while others are only discovered after close and careful investigation, the latter, once discovered, are no less certain than the former. Take, for example, the case of a right-angled triangle. Although it is not so obvious at first that the square of the base is equal to the squares of the other two sides as that the base is opposite the greatest angle, nevertheless, once it is apprehended, we are as firmly persuaded of the truth of the former as of the latter. And as for God: if I were not preoccupied by prejudices, and if my thought were not beset on all sides by the continual presence of images of sensible objects, I should know nothing sooner or more easily than the fact of his being. For is there any truth more clear than the existence of a Supreme Being, or of God, seeing that it is to his essence alone that [necessary and eternal] existence pertains?

13. And although the right conception of this truth has cost me much close thinking, nevertheless at present I am not only as assured of it as of what I deem most certain; I notice further that the certitude of all other truths so absolutely depends on it that without this knowledge it is impossible ever to know anything perfectly.

14. For although my nature is such that, while I have a very clear and distinct apprehension of a matter, I cannot resist the conviction of its truth, yet because my constitution is also such that I cannot keep my mind continually fixed on the same object, and because I frequently remember a past judgment without being able at the same time to recall the grounds of it, it may happen meanwhile that other reasons are presented to me which would readily make me change my opinion, if I did not know that God existed. And thus I would possess no true and certain knowledge, but only vague and wavering opinions. For example, when I consider the nature of the [rectilinear] triangle, it appears most clearly to me — having been instructed in the principles of geometry — that its three angles are equal to two right angles, and I find it impossible to believe otherwise while I apply my mind to the demonstration. But as soon as I stop attending to the proof, even while I still remember that I had a clear comprehension of it, I may readily come to doubt the truth demonstrated, if I do not know that there is a God: for I may persuade myself that I have been so constituted by nature as to be sometimes deceived, even in matters I think I apprehend with the greatest evidence and certitude — especially when I recall that I frequently considered many things to be true and certain which other reasons afterward forced me to reckon as wholly false.

15. But after I have discovered that God exists, since I also at the same time observed that all things depend on him, and that he is no deceiver, and from this inferred that everything I clearly and distinctly perceive is necessarily true, then, even if I no longer attend to the grounds of a judgment, no opposite reason can be alleged strong enough to make me doubt its truth, provided only I remember that I once had a clear and distinct comprehension of it. My knowledge of it thus becomes true and certain. And this same knowledge extends likewise to whatever I remember having formerly demonstrated — such as the truths of geometry and the like. For what can be alleged against them to make me doubt them? Will it be said that my nature is such that I may often be deceived? But I already know that I cannot be deceived in judgments whose grounds I clearly know. Will it be said that I formerly thought things to be true and certain which I afterward discovered to be false? But I had no clear and distinct knowledge of any of those things; and being as yet ignorant of the rule by which I am assured of the truth of a judgment, I was led to give my assent to them on grounds which I afterward discovered to be less strong than I had imagined at the time. What further objection is there? Will it be said that I am perhaps dreaming (an objection I lately raised myself), or that all the thoughts I am now conscious of have no more truth than the reveries of dreams? But even if I were dreaming, the rule still holds that all which is clearly presented to my intellect is indisputably true.

16. And thus I very clearly see that the certitude and truth of all science depends on the knowledge of the true God alone — so much so that, before I knew him, I could have no perfect knowledge of any other thing. And now that I know him, I possess the means of acquiring perfect knowledge of innumerable matters, both concerning God himself and other intellectual objects, and concerning corporeal nature insofar as it is the object of pure mathematics [which do not consider whether it exists or not].

chapters.title: Meditation VI — Of the Existence of Material Things, and of the Real Distinction Between the Mind and Body of Man
paragraphs: 1. There now remains only the inquiry whether material things exist. About this question, I at least know with certainty that such things may exist insofar as they form the object of pure mathematics, since, considered in this aspect, I can conceive them clearly and distinctly. For there can be no doubt that God has the power of producing all the objects I am able to conceive distinctly, and I never considered anything impossible to him, except when I experienced a contradiction in trying to conceive it rightly. Further, the faculty of imagination I possess, and which I am conscious of using when I apply myself to the consideration of material things, is enough to persuade me of their existence. For when I attentively consider what imagination is, I find that it is simply a certain application of the cognitive faculty (facultas cognoscitiva) to a body that is immediately present to it, and which therefore exists.

2. To make this quite clear, I note in the first place the difference between imagination and pure intellection [or conception]. For example, when I imagine a triangle I not only conceive (intelligo) that it is a figure bounded by three lines, but at the same time I look upon (intueor) these three lines as present by the power and inner application of my mind (acie mentis), and this is what I call imagining. But if I want to think of a chiliagon, I can rightly conceive that it is a figure of a thousand sides, just as easily as I conceive that a triangle is a figure of only three sides; but I cannot imagine the thousand sides of a chiliagon as I do the three sides of a triangle, nor, so to speak, view them as present [with the eyes of my mind]. And although, by my habit of always imagining something when I think of corporeal things, it may happen that, in conceiving a chiliagon, I confusedly represent some figure to myself, it is quite evident that this is not a chiliagon, since it in no way differs from what I would represent to myself if I were thinking of a myriagon, or any other figure with many sides; nor would this representation be of any use in discovering and unfolding the properties that constitute the difference between a chiliagon and other polygons. But if the question turns on a pentagon, it is quite true that I can conceive its figure, as I can that of a chiliagon, without the aid of imagination; but I can also imagine it by applying the attention of my mind to its five sides, and at the same time to the area they contain. So I observe that a special effort of the mind is needed for the act of imagination — an effort not required for conceiving or understanding (ad intelligendum); and this special exertion of the mind clearly shows the difference between imagination and pure intellection (imaginatio et intellectio pura).

3. I note further that this power of imagination, insofar as it differs from the power of conceiving, is in no way necessary to my [nature or] essence, that is, to the essence of my mind. For even if I did not possess it, I should still remain the same as I now am — from which it seems we may conclude that it depends on something different from the mind. And I easily understand that, if some body exists with which my mind is so conjoined and united that it can, as it were, consider it whenever it chooses, then it may by this means imagine corporeal objects. So this mode of thinking differs from pure intellection only in this respect: in conceiving, the mind in some way turns upon itself and considers some one of the ideas it has within itself; but in imagining, it turns toward the body, and contemplates in it some object conformed to the idea which it either conceived of itself or apprehended by sense. I easily understand, I say, that imagination may be formed this way, if it is true that bodies exist; and because I find no other obvious way to explain it, I conjecture from this with probability that they exist — but only with probability. And although I carefully examine all things, I do not find that, from the distinct idea of corporeal nature I have in my imagination, I can necessarily infer the existence of any body.

4. But I am accustomed to imagine many other objects besides that corporeal nature which is the object of pure mathematics — for example, colors, sounds, tastes, pain, and the like — though with less distinctness. And since I perceive these objects much better by the senses, through which (and through memory) they seem to have reached the imagination, I think that, in order to examine them more advantageously, I should at the same time examine what sense-perception is, and inquire whether, from those ideas which are apprehended by this mode of thinking (consciousness), I cannot obtain a certain proof of the existence of corporeal objects.

5. First, I will recall to my mind the things I have so far held as true because perceived by the senses, and the foundations on which my belief in their truth rested. Second, I will examine the reasons that afterward forced me to doubt them. And finally, I will consider what of them I ought now to believe.

6. First, then, I perceived that I had a head, hands, feet, and other limbs composing the body which I considered as part — or perhaps even as the whole — of myself. I perceived further that this body was placed among many others, by which it was capable of being affected in diverse ways, both beneficial and harmful; and what was beneficial I noted by a certain sensation of pleasure, and what was harmful by a sensation of pain. Besides this pleasure and pain, I was also conscious of hunger, thirst, and other appetites, as well as certain corporeal inclinations toward joy, sadness, anger, and similar passions. Outside myself, besides the extension, shape, and motions of bodies, I likewise perceived in them hardness, heat, and the other tactile qualities, and in addition light, colors, odors, tastes, and sounds — the variety of which gave me the means of distinguishing the sky, the earth, the sea, and generally all other bodies, from one another. And certainly, considering the ideas of all these qualities which were presented to my mind, and which alone I properly and immediately perceived, it was not without reason that I thought I perceived certain objects wholly different from my thought — namely, bodies from which those ideas proceeded. For I was conscious that the ideas were presented to me without my consent being required, so that I could not perceive any object, however much I wished to, unless it were present to the organ of sense; and it was wholly out of my power not to perceive it when it was thus present. And because the ideas I perceived by the senses were much more lively and clear, and even, in their own way, more distinct than any of those I could form for myself by meditation, or which I found impressed on my memory, it seemed that they could not have proceeded from myself, and so must have been caused in me by some other objects. And as I had no knowledge of those objects beyond what the ideas themselves gave me, nothing was so natural for my mind to suppose as that the objects were similar to the ideas they caused. And because I also recalled that I had formerly trusted the senses rather than reason, and that the ideas I myself formed were not as clear as those I perceived by sense, and that they were even for the most part composed of parts of the latter, I was readily persuaded that I had no idea in my intellect that had not formerly passed through the senses. Nor was I altogether wrong in believing that the body I called my own by a special right belonged to me more properly and strictly than any other body; for in truth I could never be separated from it as from other bodies; I felt in it and on account of it all my appetites and affections; and finally I was affected in its parts by pain and the titillation of pleasure, and not in the parts of the other bodies that were separated from it. But when I asked why, from this I-know-not-what sensation of pain, sadness of mind should follow, and why from the sensation of pleasure, joy should arise, or why this indescribable twitching of the stomach, which I call hunger, should remind me to eat, or the dryness of the throat, to drink, and so on in other cases — I could give no explanation, except that I was so taught by nature. For there is surely no affinity, at least none that I can comprehend, between this irritation of the stomach and the desire for food, any more than between the perception of an object that causes pain and the consciousness of sadness which springs from the perception. And in the same way it seemed to me that all the other judgments I had formed about the objects of sense were dictates of nature; for I observed that those judgments were formed in me before I had leisure to weigh and consider the reasons that might force me to form them.

7. But afterward a wide experience gradually undermined the trust I had placed in my senses. For I frequently observed that towers which from a distance seemed round, appeared square when more closely viewed, and that colossal figures raised on the summits of these towers looked like small statues when seen from below; and in countless other instances I found error in judgments based on the external senses — and not only those, but even in judgments based on the internal senses. For is anything more internal than pain? And yet I have sometimes been told by people whose arm or leg had been amputated that they still occasionally seemed to feel pain in the part of the body they had lost — a fact that led me to think I could not be quite certain that any one of my limbs was affected even when I felt pain in it. To these grounds for doubt I shortly afterward added two others of very wide generality. The first was that I believed there was nothing I ever perceived while awake that I could not also occasionally think I perceived while asleep; and since I do not believe that the ideas I seem to perceive in sleep proceed from objects external to me, I no longer saw any reason to believe this of those I seem to perceive when awake either. The second was that since I was as yet ignorant of the author of my being — or at least supposed myself to be — I saw nothing to prevent my having been so constituted by nature that I should be deceived even in matters that appeared to me to possess the greatest truth. And as for the grounds on which I had previously been persuaded of the existence of sensible objects, I had no great difficulty finding suitable answers to them. For since nature seemed to incline me to many things from which reason made me averse, I thought I ought not to put much trust in its teachings. And although the perceptions of the senses were not dependent on my will, I did not think I ought on that ground to conclude that they proceeded from things different from myself, since perhaps there might be in me some faculty, hitherto unknown to me, that produced them.

8. But now that I begin to know myself better, and to discover more clearly the author of my being, I do not think I should rashly admit everything the senses seem to teach; nor, on the other hand, am I convinced that I should doubt their teachings in general.

9. And first, because I know that everything I clearly and distinctly conceive can be produced by God exactly as I conceive it, it is enough that I am able clearly and distinctly to conceive one thing apart from another, in order to be certain that the one is different from the other — since they may at least be made to exist separately by the omnipotence of God; and it does not matter by what power this separation is made for me to be forced to judge them different. Therefore, simply because I know with certitude that I exist, and because in the meantime I do not observe that anything necessarily belongs to my nature or essence beyond my being a thinking thing, I rightly conclude that my essence consists only in this — that I am a thinking thing [or a substance whose whole essence or nature is merely thinking]. And although I may, or rather, as I will shortly say, although I certainly do, possess a body with which I am very closely conjoined, nevertheless, since on the one hand I have a clear and distinct idea of myself insofar as I am only a thinking and unextended thing, and on the other hand I have a distinct idea of body insofar as it is only an extended and unthinking thing, it is certain that I [that is, my mind, by which I am what I am] am entirely and truly distinct from my body, and can exist without it.

10. Moreover, I find in myself diverse faculties of thinking, each with its own special mode. For example, I find I have the faculties of imagining and of perceiving — faculties without which I can indeed clearly and distinctly conceive myself as a whole, but which, conversely, I cannot conceive without conceiving myself, that is, without an intelligent substance in which they reside; for [in the notion we have of them, or to use the terms of the schools] in their formal concept they include some kind of intellection. From this I see that they are distinct from me as modes are from things. I notice likewise certain other faculties, such as the power of changing place, of taking on diverse shapes, and the like, which cannot be conceived, and therefore cannot exist, any more than the preceding, apart from a substance in which they inhere. But it is very plain that these faculties, if they really exist, must belong to some corporeal or extended substance, since their clear and distinct concept contains some sort of extension, but no intellection at all. Further, I cannot doubt that there is in me a certain passive faculty of perception — that is, of receiving and taking knowledge of the ideas of sensible things. But this would be useless to me if there did not also exist, either in me or in some other thing, another active faculty capable of forming and producing those ideas. This active faculty cannot be in me [insofar as I am only a thinking thing], since it does not presuppose thought, and since those ideas are frequently produced in my mind without my contributing to it in any way, and even frequently against my will. This faculty must therefore exist in some substance different from me, in which all the objective reality of the ideas produced by this faculty is contained formally or eminently, as I noted before. And this substance is either a body — that is, a corporeal nature in which is contained formally [and in effect] all that is objectively [and by representation] in those ideas — or it is God himself, or some other creature of a rank superior to body, in which the same is contained eminently. But since God is no deceiver, it is plain that he does not of himself and immediately communicate those ideas to me, nor even by the intervention of any creature in which their objective reality is not formally, but only eminently, contained. For since he has given me no faculty by which I might discover this to be the case, but on the contrary a very strong inclination to believe that those ideas arise from corporeal objects, I do not see how he could be acquitted of the charge of deceit if in truth they proceeded from any other source, or were produced by causes other than corporeal things. Accordingly, it must be concluded that corporeal objects exist. Yet they are perhaps not exactly such as we perceive by the senses, for their comprehension by the senses is in many instances very obscure and confused. But it is at least necessary to admit that everything I clearly and distinctly conceive to be in them — that is, generally speaking, everything comprehended in the object of speculative geometry — really exists outside me.

11. But with respect to other things which are either only particular — for example, that the sun is of such a size and shape, etc. — or are conceived with less clearness and distinctness, such as light, sound, pain, and the like, even though they are highly dubious and uncertain, on the ground alone that God is no deceiver, and that he has consequently permitted no falsity in my opinions for which he has not also given me a faculty of correcting, I think I may safely conclude that I possess within myself the means of arriving at the truth. And, in the first place, it cannot be doubted that in each of the dictates of nature there is some truth. For by nature, considered in general, I now understand nothing more than God himself, or the order and disposition established by God in created things; and by my nature in particular I understand the assemblage of everything God has given me.

12. But there is nothing this nature teaches me more expressly [or more sensibly] than that I have a body which is ill-affected when I feel pain, and which needs food and drink when I experience the sensations of hunger and thirst, and so on. So I ought not to doubt that there is some truth in these reports.

13. Nature likewise teaches me by these sensations of pain, hunger, thirst, etc., that I am not only lodged in my body as a pilot in a vessel, but that I am besides so intimately conjoined with it, and as it were intermixed with it, that my mind and body compose a certain unity. For if this were not so, I should not feel pain when my body is hurt, since I am merely a thinking thing, but should perceive the wound by the understanding alone, just as a pilot perceives by sight when any part of his vessel is damaged. And when my body needs food or drink, I should have a clear knowledge of this, instead of being made aware of it by the confused sensations of hunger and thirst. For in truth, all these sensations of hunger, thirst, pain, and the like are nothing more than certain confused modes of thinking, arising from the union and apparent fusion of mind and body.

14. Besides this, nature teaches me that my body is surrounded by many other bodies, some of which I have to seek and others to shun. And indeed, since I perceive different sorts of colors, sounds, odors, tastes, heat, hardness, and so on, I safely conclude that there are in the bodies from which the diverse perceptions of the senses proceed certain varieties corresponding to them — although perhaps not in reality like them. And since some of these diverse perceptions of the senses are agreeable and others disagreeable, there can be no doubt that my body — or rather my entire self, insofar as I am composed of body and mind — may be variously affected, both beneficially and harmfully, by the surrounding bodies.

15. But there are many other beliefs which, though seemingly the teaching of nature, are not really so, but which obtained a place in my mind through the habit of judging things without due consideration. It may thus easily happen that such judgments contain error. For example, the opinion I have that all space in which there is nothing to affect [or make an impression on] my senses is empty; that in a hot body there is something exactly like the idea of heat in my mind; that in a white or green body there is the same whiteness or greenness which I perceive; that in a bitter or sweet body there is the same taste, and so in other cases; that the stars, towers, and all distant bodies are the same size and shape as they appear to our eyes, and so on. But to avoid any indistinctness of conception, I must accurately define what I properly understand by 'being taught by nature.' For nature is here taken in a narrower sense than when it signifies the sum of all the things God has given me. For in that broader meaning the notion includes much that belongs only to the mind [to which I am not here to be understood as referring when I use the term nature], such as the notion I have of the truth that what is done cannot be undone, and all the other truths I discern by the natural light [without the aid of the body]; and it likewise includes much that belongs only to body, and is not here covered by the term nature, such as the quality of heaviness, and the like, of which I am not speaking. The term is reserved exclusively to designate the things God has given me as a being composed of mind and body. But nature, taking the term in this sense, teaches me to shun what causes in me the sensation of pain, and to pursue what affords me the sensation of pleasure, and other things of this sort. But I do not find that it teaches me, in addition, to draw any conclusions about external objects from these diverse perceptions of the senses without a previous [careful and mature] consideration by the mind. For it is, as it appears to me, the office of the mind alone, and not of the composite whole of mind and body, to discern the truth in those matters. Thus, although the impression a star makes on my eye is no larger than the one made by a candle flame, I nevertheless feel no real or positive impulse leading me to believe that the star is no greater than the flame; the true account of the matter is simply that I have so judged from my youth, without any rational ground. And though, on approaching the fire I feel heat, and even pain on approaching it too closely, I have on this account no ground for holding that something resembling the heat I feel is in the fire, any more than for holding that there is something resembling the pain. All I have ground for believing is that there is something in it, whatever it may be, which excites in me those sensations of heat or pain. So also, although there are spaces in which I find nothing to excite or affect my senses, I must not therefore conclude that those spaces contain no body. For I see that, in this and in many other similar matters, I have been used to perverting the order of nature: these perceptions of the senses, although given me by nature merely to signify to my mind what things are beneficial and harmful to the composite whole of which it is a part — and being clear and distinct enough for that purpose — are nevertheless used by me as infallible rules by which to determine immediately the essence of bodies that exist outside me, of which they can of course afford only the most obscure and confused knowledge.

16. But I have already sufficiently considered how it happens that, despite the supreme goodness of God, there is falsity in my judgments. A difficulty, however, presents itself here regarding the things which I am taught by nature must be pursued or avoided, and also regarding the internal sensations in which I seem to have occasionally detected error [and thus to be directly deceived by nature]. For example, I may be so deceived by the agreeable taste of some dish in which poison has been mixed that I am led to take the poison. In this case, however, nature may be excused, for it simply leads me to desire the dish for its agreeable taste, and not the poison, of which it is unaware. So we can infer nothing from this circumstance beyond that our nature is not omniscient — at which there is surely no ground for surprise, since man, being of a finite nature, must likewise have a knowledge of limited perfection.

17. But we also not infrequently err in matters to which we are directly impelled by nature, as is the case with invalids who desire drink or food that would be harmful to them. It will perhaps be said here that the reason such persons are deceived is that their nature is corrupted; but this leaves the difficulty untouched, for a sick man is no less truly the creature of God than a man in full health, and therefore it is as repugnant to the goodness of God for the nature of the former to be deceitful as for that of the latter. And just as a clock made of wheels and counterweights observes all the laws of nature no less accurately when it is ill made and indicates the hours incorrectly, than when it satisfies the maker's design in every respect, so likewise, if the body of man is considered as a kind of machine, so made up and composed of bones, nerves, muscles, veins, blood, and skin that, even if there were no mind in it, it would still exhibit the same motions which it now manifests involuntarily — and therefore without the aid of the mind [and simply by the dispositions of its organs] — I easily see that it would also be as natural for such a body, supposing it dropsical, for example, to experience the dryness of the throat that is usually accompanied in the mind by the sensation of thirst, and to be disposed by this dryness to move its nerves and other parts in the way required for drinking, and so increase its illness and harm itself, as it is natural for it, when it is not unwell, to be stimulated to drink for its good by a similar cause. And although, looking to the use for which a clock was destined by its maker, I may say that it is deflected from its proper nature when it inaccurately indicates the hours, and on the same principle, considering the machine of the human body as having been formed by God for the sake of the motions which it usually manifests, I may likewise have ground for thinking that it does not follow the order of its nature when the throat is parched and drinking does not tend to its preservation, I nevertheless plainly see that this latter sense of the term nature is very different from the other. For the latter is nothing more than a certain denomination, depending entirely on my thought (and hence called extrinsic), by which I compare a sick man and an imperfectly constructed clock with the idea I have of a man in good health and a well-made clock. The other sense of nature, by contrast, designates something truly found in things, and therefore possessing some truth.

18. But certainly, although in respect of a dropsical body it is only by way of exterior denomination that we say its nature is corrupted when, without needing drink, the throat is parched, yet in respect of the composite whole — that is, of the mind in its union with the body — it is not a pure denomination, but really an error of nature, for it to feel thirst when drink would be harmful. And so it remains to be considered why it is that the goodness of God does not prevent the nature of man, taken in this way, from being fallacious.

19. To begin this examination, I note in the first place that there is a vast difference between mind and body, in this respect: that body, by its nature, is always divisible, and that mind is entirely indivisible. For in truth, when I consider the mind — that is, when I consider myself only insofar as I am a thinking thing — I can distinguish in myself no parts; rather, I very clearly see that I am something absolutely one and entire. And although the whole mind seems to be united to the whole body, when a foot, an arm, or any other part is cut off, I am conscious that nothing has been taken from my mind. Nor can the faculties of willing, perceiving, conceiving, and so on, properly be called its parts; for it is the same mind that is exercised [all entire] in willing, in perceiving, and in conceiving. But quite the opposite holds for corporeal or extended things; for I cannot imagine any one of them [however small it may be] which I cannot easily divide in thought, and which I therefore do not know to be divisible. This alone would be enough to teach me that the mind, or soul, of man is entirely different from the body, even if I had not already been informed of it on other grounds.

20. I note, in the next place, that the mind does not immediately receive impressions from all the parts of the body, but only from the brain — or perhaps even from one small part of it, namely, the part where the common sense (sensus communis) is said to reside. As often as this part is affected in the same way, it gives rise to the same perception in the mind, even though meanwhile the other parts of the body may be variously disposed, as is shown by innumerable experiments which it is unnecessary to enumerate here.

21. I note, besides, that the nature of body is such that no part of it can be moved by another part a little distance away without that intermediate part being capable of being moved in the same way by any of the parts that lie between the two — even though the most remote part does not act at all. For example, in a cord A, B, C, D [which is in tension], if its last part D is pulled, the first part A will not be moved differently than it would be were one of the intermediate parts B or C to be pulled, while the last part D meanwhile remained fixed. And in the same way, when I feel pain in the foot, the science of physics teaches me that this sensation is experienced by means of the nerves dispersed over the foot, which, extending like cords from it to the brain, when contracted in the foot, contract at the same time the inmost parts of the brain in which they have their origin, and excite in those parts a certain motion appointed by nature to cause in the mind a sensation of pain, as if existing in the foot. But since these nerves must pass through the tibia, the leg, the loins, the back, and the neck in order to reach the brain, it may happen that, although their extremities in the foot are not affected, but only certain of their parts that pass through the loins or neck, the same movements are nevertheless excited in the brain by this motion as would have been caused there by a hurt received in the foot. And so the mind will necessarily feel pain in the foot, just as if it had been hurt; and the same is true of all the other perceptions of our senses.

22. I note, finally, that since each of the movements made in the part of the brain by which the mind is immediately affected impresses it with only a single sensation, the most likely supposition is that this movement causes the mind to experience, among all the sensations it is capable of producing, the one that is best fitted, and generally most useful, for the preservation of the human body when it is in full health. Experience shows us that all the perceptions nature has given us are of the kind I have mentioned; and accordingly, there is nothing found in them that does not manifest the power and goodness of God. Thus, for example, when the nerves of the foot are violently or unusually shaken, the motion that passes through the medulla of the spine to the innermost parts of the brain provides a sign to the mind on which it experiences a sensation — namely, of pain, as if it were in the foot — by which the mind is warned and prompted to do its utmost to remove the cause as dangerous and harmful to the foot. It is true that God could have so constituted the nature of man that the same motion in the brain would have informed the mind of something altogether different: the motion might, for example, have been the occasion for the mind to become conscious of itself, insofar as it is in the brain, or in some place intermediate between the foot and the brain, or, finally, the occasion for it to perceive some other object entirely, whatever it might be. But none of these alternatives would have contributed as well to the preservation of the body as does what the mind actually feels. In the same way, when we need drink, there arises from this need a certain dryness in the throat that moves its nerves, and through them the internal parts of the brain; and this movement affects the mind with the sensation of thirst, because on that occasion there is nothing more useful for us than to be made aware that we need drink for the preservation of our health; and so on in other instances.

23. From this it is quite plain that, despite the sovereign goodness of God, the nature of man, insofar as it is composed of mind and body, cannot but be sometimes fallacious. For if there is any cause that excites — not in the foot, but in some part of the nerves that stretch from the foot to the brain, or even in the brain itself — the same movement that is ordinarily produced when the foot is ill affected, pain will be felt as if in the foot, and the sense will thus be naturally deceived. For since the same movement in the brain can only impress the mind with the same sensation, and since this sensation is much more frequently excited by a cause that hurts the foot than by one acting elsewhere, it is reasonable that it should lead the mind to feel pain in the foot rather than in some other part of the body. And if it sometimes happens that the parched throat does not arise, as usual, from drink being necessary for the health of the body, but from quite the opposite cause, as is the case with the dropsical, yet it is far better that it should be deceptive in that instance than if, on the contrary, it were continually fallacious when the body is in good condition; and the same holds in other cases.

24. And certainly this consideration is of great service, not only in enabling me to recognize the errors to which my nature is liable, but likewise in making it easier to avoid or correct them. For, knowing that all my senses indicate to me what is true more often than what is false in matters relating to the advantage of the body — and being able almost always to make use of more than a single sense in examining the same object — and besides this, being able to use my memory to connect present with past knowledge, and my understanding, which has already discovered all the causes of my errors, I ought no longer to fear that falsity may be found in what is daily presented to me by the senses. And I ought to reject all the doubts of those past days as hyperbolical and ridiculous — especially the general uncertainty about sleep, which I could not distinguish from the waking state. For I now find a very marked difference between the two: our memory can never connect our dreams with each other, and with the course of life, in the way it usually does with events that occur when we are awake. And in truth, if someone, while I am awake, appeared to me all of a sudden and as suddenly disappeared, as do the images I see in sleep, so that I could not observe either where he came from or where he went, I should not unreasonably regard him as a specter or phantom formed in my brain, rather than a real man. But when I perceive objects with regard to which I can distinctly determine both the place from which they come and the place where they are, and the time at which they appear to me, and when, without interruption, I can connect my perception of them with the whole of the other parts of my life, I am perfectly sure that what I thus perceive occurs while I am awake and not during sleep. And I ought not in the slightest to doubt the truth of these presentations, if, after having brought together all my senses, my memory, and my understanding to examine them, no testimony is given by any one of these faculties that contradicts that of any other. For since God is no deceiver, it necessarily follows that I am not deceived in this. But because the necessities of action frequently oblige us to make a decision before we have had leisure for so careful an examination, it must be confessed that the life of man is frequently liable to error with respect to particular objects; and we must, in conclusion, acknowledge the weakness of our nature.
